Latest Update: Tesla Cybercab Is Now Available for Purchase for $29,990, Plus $299 a Month to Use It

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (403 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk once promised the fully autonomous, steering-wheel- and pedal-free Tesla Cybercab would arrive before the year 2027, and start at less than $30,000.
  • In a recent development, cybercab pricing starts at $29,990, a price that includes the first month of the autonomy subscription required to operate the vehicle; every subsequent month, however, users will need to pay $299 for that subscription.
  • But, as the saying goes, there’s a catch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk once promised the fully autonomous, steering-wheel- and pedal-free Tesla Cybercab would arrive before the year 2027, and start at less than $30,000. Prominent tech influencer Marques Brownlee promised back in 2024 to shave his head if Tesla delivered on that cost and timeline. It appears that the automaker, very technically, has done so, as Tesla unveiled on X on Friday evening that “select customers” can now purchase a Cybercab through an early-access, limited-release program.

In a recent development, cybercab pricing starts at $29,990, a price that includes the first month of the autonomy subscription required to operate the vehicle; every subsequent month, however, users will need to pay $299 for that subscription. Customers can reserve a Cybercab with a non-refundable $1000 deposit. Deliveries in Austin, Texas will begin in December 2026.

But, as the saying goes, there’s a catch. The first one here is that owners can only operate the Tesla Cybercab in areas where it has been approved for use. According to Tesla’s website, that presently includes major cities in two states: Austin, San Antonio, Dallas-Fort Worth, and Houston in Texas, and Tampa Bay, Orlando, and Miami in Florida. Tesla’s website lists Las Vegas, Phoenix, and Jacksonville as “coming soon.”.

Recent findings suggest that another restriction is that Tesla is not selling the Cybercab to fleet operators—the most obvious customer—just yet. Customers in this initial batch may purchase one Cybercab, and only for personal use. However, Tesla does have an interest form that potential fleet operators can fill out on its website.

Sources indicate that the Cybercab and autonomous driving in general represent potentially game-changing technology—a major reason automakers and major tech companies have invested heavily and worked on it for more than a decade. In theory, Tesla and third-party operators could offer incredibly low ride-sharing prices, with no driver who needs to be compensated with humane wages. Prices would be low enough not just to undercut rideshare providers such as Uber and Lyft, but potentially to undermine personal vehicle ownership itself.

In a recent development, but achieving that Tesla-driven utopia may be a far-off prospect. To change the game, the technology must work. As Jeremy Clarkson and others have noted, Tesla’s Cybercab ride-sharing service still has several kinks to work out. Broad regulatory approval remains a relatively distant prospect. And even if the technology works and meets safety standards, customers still have to buy in.

Is Your Obsession Actually Limerence?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • Industry observers note that the experience and expression of human attachment is complex, to say the least.
  • According to recent reports, are you someone who obsesses about others?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Industry observers note that the experience and expression of human attachment is complex, to say the least. As humans, we may share a universal ingrained wiring for connection, but how we navigate this interpersonal world is not the same from person to person.

According to recent reports, are you someone who obsesses about others? Maybe you understand infatuation in the early stages of love, but then know how to transition to a mutual relationship or let go? Forming steady and stable connections is easy for some people; others are tortured with intense and uncertain attachments. New research provides insight into limerence, a specific form of intense attachment that is starting to gain more attention.

Industry observers note that imagine someone fixating on another person. This isn't hard to do. We hear about it on podcasts, watch it unfold in fantastic crime dramas, and, of course, some of us experience it in real life. From infatuation to unrequited love, examples of preoccupations with another person, outside of established relationships, color the romantic landscape. Limerence, however, is different.

Limerence is an intense and highly disruptive cognitive and emotional experience (Marshall et al., 2025; Tennov, 1979). Individuals in the throes of limerence are overwhelmed by the desire to be viewed positively by a specific someone else (i.e., the limerence object). This obsession manifests as uncontrollable rumination to the point that it interferes with day-to-day life.

Recent findings suggest that limerence is typically expressed toward someone with whom the experiencer is highly unlikely to form a real relationship. On the surface, this might seem like unrequited love, but it is far more intense and generally less realistic.

From a case study analysis, Wyant (2021) offered the following pathway by which people might come to experience limerence:.

A recent review (Bradbury et al., 2025) summarized a step-wise sequence proposed by Verhulst (1984). This model suggests that limerence begins in the context of need: a person's needs for emotional intimacy, support, and connection are not fulfilled in their current relationships. Limerence can follow from there:.

In a recent development, different dimensions of limerence are predictable by key psychological constructs. Recent research suggests limerence is best understood as a two-dimensional construct, comprised of both an intense need for attachment and neglect of self or others (Marshall et al., 2025).

Attachment anxiety, imaginative fantasy (i.e., the tendency to daydream), and the need to belong are linked to the need-for-attachment dimension of limerence for those experiencing it. This dimension is also predicted by psychological inflexibility and emotional dependence, obsessive preoccupation, self-conscious anxiety, and idealization (Marshall et al., 2025). The neglect dimension operates similarly, except it is not predicted by attachment orientation or idealization, and is associated with more social anxiety and lower self-esteem.

Whereas scholars have noted parallels between limerence and addiction and noted the potential path from limerence to stalking (e.g., Bradbury et al., 2025), there's reason to suggest that limerence can also serve as a coping mechanism in an unfulfilling relational context. Experiencing limerence can be a one-time experience or repeated, short-lived or long (Tennov, 1979), yet the context in which it occurs offers the suggestion that it is the mind's way of addressing an undermet need for belonging and intimacy. The field has much more to learn about limerence as an unusual manifestation of the human attachment system.

Sources indicate that bradbury, P., Short, E., & Bleakley, P. (2025). Limerence, hidden obsession, fixation, and rumination: A scoping review of human behaviour. Journal of Police and Criminal Psychology, 40(2), 417-426.

Marshall, L., Waldeck, D., Pancani, L., Churchill, S., & Tyndall, I. (2025). Development and validation of the Limerence Questionnaire (LQ-11). Psychological reports, 00332941251394980.

Industry observers note that verhulst, J. (1984). Limerence: Notes on the nature and function of passionate love. Psychoanalysis & Contemporary Thought, 7(1), 115–138.

Sources indicate that wyant, B. E. (2021). Treatment of limerence using a cognitive behavioral approach: A case study. Journal of patient experience, 8, 23743735211060812.

#109853. Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system.
  • Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.
  • Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to new analysis from energy think tank Ember.

Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.

Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.

The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup.

Solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls.

That matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that in the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12.

The savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%.

“We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” stated Daan Walter, principal at Ember.

In a recent development, by combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy.

In a recent development, the researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years.

Industry observers note that that’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average.

Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output.

The findings also raise questions for developers planning new fossil fuel plants.

Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%.

In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper.

Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW.

For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics.

Good way to think about the whole system. So what exactly does Don not-Quixote have against windmills?

Ember’s interactive Wind + Solar + Battery Atlas lets users explore reliable electricity costs in their own region.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that AHEAD OF THE fall, I knew I was going to need a sickening boot that could just fall in line with my entire wardrobe. I don’t spend much on clothes, because, well, I wear-test them for a living, but when it comes to shopping for footwear I’ve been guilty of dropping more bread than I’d like to admit. There are times I don’t mind dishing out a little cash for a well-made shoe, especially if that means I’ll have it for years to come. One style that was calling my name that I couldn’t resist was Our Legacy’s Camion Boot.

Sources indicate that if you’ve spent any time scrolling through men’s fashion content on Instagram or TikTok, chances are you’ve come across it. Even actor Paul Mescal has been spotted wearing the boot during a press tour for “Hamnet” in London. The sleek leather ankle-high boot has become something of a cult favorite among stylish guys, thanks to its distinctive square toe and minimalist design, which helps make any simple outfit look 10 times cooler. Whether I’m wearing baggy jeans or relaxed trousers, The Camion Boot adds a certain je ne sais quoi that my cowboy or lace-up boots can’t replicate. And by no means does the boot feel squishy like your favorite pair of sneakers, but the Vibram rubber outsole keeps my feet comfortable on days when I'm standing and walking around for hours.

For those unfamiliar, Our Legacy is a Swedish fashion label founded in Stockholm in 2005. Over the past two decades, the brand has built a loyal following for taking menswear staples and remixing them with unique proportions, fabrics, and details. The Camion Boot is one of its most recognizable designs, decorated with an inside zip closure and a metal branded tab. It feels timeless without looking boring. Even though it’s easy on the eyes, its $700-plus price tag is tough on the wallet. Luckily, you don’t have to cough up designer money to get the look. Below, I’ve gathered a list of affordable alternatives that deliver the same vibe for a fraction of the price.

If you’re looking for a boot that captures the sleek appeal of Our Legacy’s Camion without spending a small fortune, Florsheim’s Medford is a strong contender. The leather upper has a subtle burnished finish that delivers a slightly worn-in look, as the clean silhouette makes it easy to dress up or down. I’d pair the brown version with black denim and a chunky sweater for dinner followed by a night out. It also looks sharp with dressy pants and tailored trousers, so you can get plenty of mileage out of it at the office.

Recent findings suggest that inside, there’s a fully cushioned, removable footbed made with OrthoLite rebound foam, which helps absorb impact and provides a little extra bounce underfoot. This comes in handy if you’re spending hours on your feet. The leather is also designed to feel comfortable from the jump, so you shouldn’t have to suffer through a lengthy break-in period. And while I wouldn’t treat these like rain boots, the leather construction makes them a practical choice for everyday wear, especially with proper care. You don’t have to settle for a black colorway either—it comes in a few different brown shades as well.

Zara offers a squared-off toe that is unapologetically bold, giving the boot that exaggerated, fashion-forward shape that makes Our Legacy’s Camion so recognizable. I’d argue the toe is even more pronounced here, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing if you want your footwear to stand out more. I’d style these with relaxed jeans that fall just over the shaft or wide-leg trousers to really lean into the silhouette.

The biggest difference comes down to the material. Unlike the Camion, Zara’s version is made from polyurethane, a synthetic material that mimics the appearance of leather, so it’s a budget-friendly pick. It’s generally easy to wipe clean, but it won’t develop the same natural patina as genuine leather and can eventually peel or crack with repeated wear.

Industry observers note that steve Madden’s Ronco might be the closest style to the Camion boot as far as design is concerned. It nailed the features from the stitched detailing across the upper right down to the substantial rubber sole. The latter is worth pointing out because it gives the boot a similar sturdy, grounded appearance, while the 1.5-inch heel adds just enough height without going overboard. Sure, the rounded toe isn’t quite as boxy as the Camion’s signature square shape, but the overall silhouette comes pretty darn close. And at a fraction of the price, it’s hard not to appreciate the resemblance.

In a recent development, I’m especially drawn to the brown leather version, which has a rich, burnished finish that shifts between lighter and darker shades, giving it a slightly weathered, vintage effect. It has a lot more depth than your standard brown boot. I’d pair these with relaxed denim and a chunky sweater for an easy apple-picking look, or throw them on with tailored trousers and a leather jacket for something a little sharper. There’s also a black option if you prefer to keep things simple.

Banana Republic takes a different approach with this Italian leather Chelsea-style boot. The silhouette is sleek and understated, but what really caught my attention is the leather’s distressed finish. It has that subtly weathered, almost cracked appearance you’d normally expect from a well-loved pair of boots, except the detail is already built into the design. It gives the shoe a vintage feel without looking like something that’s been sitting in the back of your closet for a decade. I also appreciate that this pair doesn’t try too hard to replicate the Camion. Instead, it offers a more classic interpretation that feels right at home with the rest of my wardrobe. I’d wear it with pleated trousers and a button-down for the office, then swap in straight-leg jeans and a crewneck for a day of shopping.

According to recent reports, camper has a knack for taking classic footwear and giving it a slightly unexpected twist, which perfectly describes the Dean Boot. The black-and-burgundy color combination immediately caught my attention because it’s subtle enough to wear with anything, but there’s also a richness to the pebbled leather texture that makes it more interesting than your standard black ankle boot. I’d pair these with relaxed black trousers or dark denim and let the boots bring a little personality to the outfit.

In a recent development, the upper combines calfskin leather with recycled PET, which is plastic recycled from materials like water bottles, and latex for added flexibility. Underfoot, there’s a removable OrthoLite footbed for cushioning and an XL Extralight EVA outsole, a lightweight foam-based material designed to absorb impact without weighing you down. I also appreciate the pull tab, which makes slipping them on a little easier, especially since there’s no traditional side zipper. Plus, the defined heel and outsole design offer some stability for walking, though actual traction will depend on the surface.

Sources indicate that I’ve owned my Frye boots for about a year now, and they’ve more than earned their place in my footwear rotation. They’re so versatile, I can wear them with a suit one day and jeans, a T-shirt, and leather jacket the next. The design is minimal with a premium leather upper and stitching around the edge that adds to the sturdy construction. Comfort-wise, I didn’t have to deal with that annoying break-in period that often comes with leather boots.

After a year of wear, the leather has started developing some natural creases, but I look at it like it adds character. There’s enough wiggle room in the toe box that my feet don’t feel cramped. The inner side zipper is another detail I’ve come to appreciate, especially when I’m taking them off after a long day. I’ve put these through their paces on city streets and even worn them in the rain. I found the leather has dried rapidly after getting wet, and the grip has felt secure underfoot. Sure, they’re not cheap, but considering how well they’ve held up and how often I wear them, I’d say I’ve already gotten my money’s worth.

According to recent reports, if you’re a guy who gets suited up more often than not, Suitsupply’s leather boot deserves a spot on your radar. It’s the dressiest option on this list, with a smooth, semi-matte leather, which catches just enough light to look sharp without being overly shiny. It also has a fine, tight grain, which gives the surface a supple finish. I’d wear these with a charcoal suit or tailored black trousers and a crisp button-down, for a holiday party. But I would also style them with dark denim and a cashmere sweater. The side zipper makes getting dressed a little less of a production in the morning. The leather sole adds to that dress-shoe appeal, although I’d be a little more cautious wearing these on slick pavement.

Industry observers note that now, these are the most expensive boots on this list, but because they’re made in Italy using Blake-stitched construction, a technique that stitches the upper directly to the sole for a slimmer, more flexible profile than you’d typically get with bulkier boot construction. You can expect some natural creasing after a few wears, particularly where your foot bends, but that doesn’t mean the leather is cracking.

It has been revealed that to keep it from drying out, Suitsupply recommends applying shoe polish at least once a month, or more frequently if you’re wearing them daily. This helps maintain the color and adds some protection against moisture. I’d also work in a leather conditioner whenever the material starts feeling dry to help prevent actual cracking. It’s a little extra maintenance, sure, but worthwhile if you’re investing this much in a pair of boots.

It’s served me well on daily commutes, errand runs, and neighborhood walks.

Industry observers note that this carry-on is a splurge at $945, but its lifetime warranty and anodized aluminum shell mean it will last for many journeys, even after some rough-and-tumble handling from baggage people (that just adds personalized patina). It has TSA-compliant locks to stop snooping eyes and prevents the bag from bursting mid-flight. The 360-degree silent wheels let you drag or roll this luggage however you please. We also love this carry-on for its plentiful storage, including a zippered garment compartment and two internal pockets. A built-in compression pad with straps helps compact overpacking.

Industry observers note that this $200 backpack from Thule is my go-to travel backpack and is my most-used personal item. It fits easily under seats and comes with a chest strap, water bottle holder, and a stowable divider with TPU lining that’s excellent for keeping dirty clothes separate from the clean ones. The back panel fully unzips, letting me open the backpack fully like a suitcase. And I can rest easy knowing my electronics are protected in the plush 17-inch laptop and tablet sleeves. Its water-resistant finish keeps my wares dry in the rain, and the expandable middle section gives me more wiggle room when I’ve overpacked and lets me compress the goods when the bag is full.

Gear and Commerce Editor Tony Ware, meanwhile, is a huge fan of the 27L TuffSkin YETI Ranchero, which sports a Y-shaped easy-pull RipZip Opening in the front that provides full access to the pack’s main compartment and internal pockets, plus the GroundControl Base that ensures it stands upright when put down. He’s taken it from DC to Hawaii, Europe, and Asia packed with two laptops, a stuffed Peak Design Tech Pouch, sometimes multiple headphones, and more, and it’s the most reliable carry-on he’s tried.

Industry observers note that this $395 piece of checked luggage from Monos is made from a durable, aerospace-grade polycarbonate shell, making it practically unbreakable and resistant to water and dents after hard impacts with walls, poles, and floors. The wraparound zipper adds almost two inches of depth, so you can pack an extra outfit or two (or bring back souvenirs). Handy features like a telescopic handle, whisper-quiet wheels, and a TSA-accepted lock allow for easy movin’ throughout the airport. Even the included freebies are practical: The roller luggage comes with an anti-microbial, silver ion-coated laundry bag, two shoe bags, and a vegan leather luggage tag.

The $219 40-Liter Baboon to the Moon Go-Bag is my duffel bag of choice for weekend trips or pet-sitting stints. I’ve gotten my money’s worth out of my baby pink bag, which has been by my side at conferences in Chicago, trade highlights in Nevada, jaunts to Washington, D.C., and Philadelphia for concerts, and train rides to my hometown. Wherever she goes, I follow, thanks to a water-repellent coating, stash pockets, and—best of all—her agreeableness with TSA or gate agents as a carry-on. B2TM (the abbreviated name for the organization) added a laptop sleeve and compression straps to its most recent version of the Go-Bag, meaning I can ditch my laptop backpack and pack smarter than ever, AKA: I can shove more crap in there. It will be a while before my Go-Bag goes to suitcase heaven; when it does, I will be ready to throw down my credit card to get a replacement.

Industry observers note that the $118 Halfday Garment Duffel makes the most of every bit of space. It unfurls to resemble a traditional zippered garment bag, with included hanger loops and a strap to prevent clothing from falling out. Zip up the sides to shape it into a duffel bag, and add shoes, jeans, and accessories. It’s carry-on compliant for most airlines, and comes with a trolley sleeve to slide over a suitcase handle. Consider it a go-to for business travel, weddings, and weekend trips. Mary Poppins would be jealous.

The $54 Thule Compression Cube Set turns days of outfits into a compact, stowable rectangle. I use the medium cube for T-shirts, jeans, and leggings, and keep smaller items, like socks, bras, and underwear, in the smaller cube. I don’t travel without these cubes, and they’ve held up.

Don’t be blindsided by overweight luggage with this $10 portable bag scale from travel inspira. It’s easy to use: Switch between tare weight, kilograms, and pounds with the press of a button. The LCD display is easy to read, and the rubberized handle keeps hands comfortable while weighing bags. An auto-off feature preserves battery power, and a low battery indicator indicates when it’s time for a replacement. A 110-lb. weight capacity accommodates even the heaviest luggage.

Industry observers note that unlike other luggage tags, the $8 Ovener Silicone Luggage Tag has a built-in metal rivet and steel loop, meaning it won’t stretch out, snap, or tear. Its flexible silicone adds to its durability, and a name window helps rapidly identify luggage without revealing too much to prying eyes. Nine total colors add personality and help a suitcase stand out. It comes in a pack of two—no bag left untagged!

If you’re shopping for someone who loves something super personalized, beyond just color, the $19 Grommet Bag Tag from Visitag is for them. You can customize the front and back, or just the front: choose from 12 tag colors, six emoji locations (for an extra $2.50 per emoji), 12 characters of embroidered front-and-back text, and 17 thread colors for the embroidery on either side of the tag. The ID card is located inside the bag tag, giving just enough privacy. Durable and fun, and a way to make your suitcase stand out from every other spinner on the carousel … what more could someone want in a travel gift!?!

The $29 Apple AirTag is a savior to anyone who has ever lost a device or bag. Its precise tracking makes it even easier than before to find bags; a louder speaker and redesigned chime help with the hunt. Consider upgrading to a four-pack to cover all your bags. The Chipolo Loop Rechargeable Bluetooth Tracker is a great Bluetooth tracker for Android phones, or any phone really, thanks to its universal compatibility with Apple Find My or Google’s Find Hub.

I’ve used this $38 BAGGU 3D Zip Set to store extra cords, emergency must-haves like Band-Aids and hand sanitizer, and to keep shoes separate from clothes. My favorite use for these utilitarian pouches is stowing all my goops and other toiletries. The large pouch expands to 10 inches by 7 inches; the medium one expands to 8.5 inches by 5 inches; and the smallest expands to 7 inches by 3 inches. Recycled ripstop nylon means I don’t have to be so gentle with these durable pouches, and they’re machine washable, a must for cleaning up rogue spills.

It has been revealed that these $40 Matador FlatPak Toiletry Bottles hold 90 milliliters of volume at half the bulk, so you’ll have enough shampoo, body wash, conditioner, and lotion for the entire trip. Flip the cap to dispense, and unscrew it to access the large fill opening. These space-saving travel bottles are five times lighter and almost four times more compact compared to their silicone counterparts. We also love the manufacturer’s Waterproof Canister to protect vitamins, pills, 1ml/2ml travel scents, and other small bits.

Recent findings suggest that this $40, 16-ounce bottle from Zojirushi is just as high-quality and reliable as the manufacturer’s rice cookers (another gift we love to give). It features an electropolished SlickSteel interior that resists stains and prevents corrosion, plus a safety lock that prevents spills from accidental lid openings. An air vent on the mouthpiece lets water flow down the sip spout without gushing or overflowing, lessening the risk of spills. And one has kept our hot and cold beverages at a pleasant temperature for entire transcontinental flights. Looking for a bit more capacity? This bottle is also available in a 20-ounce size.

Sources indicate that the $129 LARQ PureVis 2 significantly improves on its original PureVis bottle, which we reviewed in 2023. It now comes with USB-C charging, water intake tracking, and a filter straw that reduces chlorine, VOCs, and PFAS (PFOA/PFOS). It still includes powerful UV-C LED purification that runs every two hours and eliminates 99% of biocontaminants like E. Coli from your water and bottle. The Advanced filter tackles everything from the essential filter, along with haloacetic acids (HAAs, a disinfection byproduct), lead, and flame retardants, with an increased filter life of 40 gallons. Double-wall insulation keeps drinks cold for 24 hours, making it excellent for long travels. Choose from 23 or 34 ounces.

The $38 VIM & VIGR 15-20 mmHg Merino Wool Graduated Compression Socks help improve blood flow and reduce leg achiness after hours in a pressurized cabin. Plus, the merino wool naturally regulates temperature, wicks moisture, and resists odor, making these a double-whammy for comfort. These compression socks are also ideal for hiking and make a great gift for anyone who spends a lot of time on their feet. VIM & VIGR creates compression socks with fun designs, because life is too short for boring socks.

The Trtl Men’s Travel Hoodie is a $140 sweatshirt designed for long flights in chilly cabins or cross-country car trips in the cooler months. It may look like a regular hoodie with a kangaroo pocket, but a closer look reveals travel-focused features. It comes with a large zippered pocket and two smaller pockets that secure keys, headphones, phones, and a passport while keeping them within reach. Other travel-friendly features include a triple-layer hood that softens sounds in loud environments (e.g., Baby on Plane, Man with Undiagnosed Sleep Apnea Snoring, Bachelorette Fallout, etc.), lower armholes for easy removal in tight spaces, and no neck tags for comfort. And yes, it has thumbholes! Pair this travel hoodie with our favorite neck pillow and/or some noise-canceling headphones (keep scrolling for suggestions) for a perfect nap in transit.

Recent findings suggest that between cabin pressure and whatever passes for a meal in economy, a man’s guts may be going through things before you reach the gate (as a vegetarian often fed chickpeas and/or lentils, I’m speaking from experience). Well, these $109 pants were made for that, and other things. The four-way stretch fabric, with 11% elastane, plus a laser-perforated panel across the back let out the heat while you’re stuck in your seat. And a hidden elastic waist and drawstring keep the pants up without having to worry about a belt that might slow things down going through security (though Roark did add belt loops in case you have to rush to a more upscale dinner when you land). But wait, there’s more! Zip pockets can secure a passport, and a stash pocket in the back is deep enough for a phone when you’re fumbling with luggage. We’ve worn a pair from DC to Kona, as well as Atlanta to Tokyo, and would highly recommend them over sweatpants if you’re looking for long-haul comfort (particularly to warmer destinations) that lets you look more put together. And, while Roark doesn’t make these specific pants in a women’s style, they do have other options.

Recent findings suggest that TSA may have loosened its shoes-off security rules, so you may not have to loosen your laces. But like everything when flying, that’s subject to change (especially if you get pulled aside for an extra screening). Plus, even if you can keep them on in the airport, you might want to take them off somewhere over the ocean. And if you’ve ever tried to tie your shoes again in a cramped economy row, you know it requires some contortionist skills. Not with Kizik shoes. The laces are just for looks. The shoes are designed so the heel compresses as you slip your foot in, then springs back into place (up to 30,000 times a pair). Some have a disguised mechanism, while others (like the $129 Athens 2 above, available in many colorways) show the compression cage. And they’re comfortable from Day One, thanks to the breathable stretch-knit upper (or soft leather on the Vegas 2), insole, and rocker sole/high-rebound midsole, which helps as you rush through a connection or explore a city. So go ahead, kick those shoes off when the seatbelt sign goes off.

In a recent development, the $149 Purple Harmony Anywhere Pillow is for those who are picky about where they rest their head while counting Z’s, whether it’s in a hotel, on a friend’s couch, or while roughing it outdoors. The pillow packs luxury in a compact size: the Honeycomb GelFlex Grid and Talalay latex core keep the pillow firm and cool, while giving plenty of neck support. A moisture-wicking mesh cover keeps things airy, because a hot pillow makes for unhappy travels. Need something more targeted for those long hours in 32C? The Purple Back Pillow is great for portable lumbar support, and has made multiple overnight flights more bearable for us.

Plane cabins and train cars can get chilly; the $90 Rumpl Travel Puffy Blanket balances warmth and comfort with packability. In fact, it’s almost as large as a throw blanket and packs down to the size of a 32-ounce water bottle (shown above for perspective, but not included). Even better, it easily clips onto a backpack. Choose from sunset-inspired shades or your favorite solid color to show off your style while keeping cozy.

In a recent development, these $359 Bose QuietComfort Headphones make an excellent, practical gift and are essential for travel: Planes and trains can be noisy, and playing your media sans headphones is a party foul on every mode of transportation. Bose makes some of the best noise-canceling headphones for airplane travel, from over-ear models to true wireless earbuds. This updated model comes with pill-shaped earcups, a 24-hour battery life, Immersive Audio, QuietControl noise cancellation that mutes practically all outside sound, and updated ActiveSense Tech to smooth sound spikes in Aware Mode.

Not everyone likes substantial over-ear headphones (like the Bose above), or the feeling and more limited battery life of true wireless earbuds. Well, Marshall has a solution: The $229 on-ear Milton A.N.C. Bluetooth 6.0 headphones, which bring active noise cancellation to a less typical form factor. Six microphones feed the adaptive noise canceling, which is surprisingly effective despite not having the benefit of a complete seal around the ear. Plus, a charge lasts 50 hours with ANC on, and 15 minutes plugged in can get you 9.5 hours more, so Upcoming York to Singapore and back ain’t a thang. And adaptive loudness/EQ/spatial audio settings help give those days in the air even more vibes. There’s a USB-C-to-3.5mm cable for wired listening (just remember your seatback entertainment system adapter, and to have the headphones charged because they don’t run passively). They fold up and only weigh 200 grams, so they’re perfect in an already-stuffed personal item, maybe even a jacket pocket. And they’ve got that classic Marshall cool, all textured, leather-like vinyl with brass logo/control knobs. You’ll be rockin’ even when you’re not walkin’ ….

Sources indicate that we haven’t met wireless earbuds that haven’t announced “battery low” at some point before a flight ended, which isn’t optimal, especially if an attempt at getting some sleep is involved. But these $99 Bose wired earbuds will never give you up, never let you down, never get run down and desert you. Run off the USB-C port of any smartphone, tablet, or laptop, these bring back a newtro style Bose hasn’t made in a decade. And they are unlikely to discontinue it again anytime soon, considering the overwhelming positive response. Using the proprietary QuietControl algorithms that make other Sound By Bose products so good, they cut most perceived noise while providing a convenient three-button in-line remote that switches between Quiet, Aware, and off modes, plus offers playback controls. Plus, multiple eartip-and-stability band size combinations ensure a secure fit. And even if one comes loose on the way in/out of the included case, the 4.2-foot cable means you won’t have that moment of terror that an earbud rolled three rows back.

In a recent development, this $80 Anker Universal Charger combines compatibility with outlets from more than 200 countries into one power block charger. It detects local voltage in one second and is Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory (NRTL)-certified for safe, stable charging. Unlike other international outlet adapters, this one is 25% smaller and designed to stay securely plugged in. And its USB-C/USB-A ports can charge four devices at once, including tech that requires higher voltage, like laptops and tablets.

Recent findings suggest that no outlet is guaranteed in this world, but Anker’s $135 Laptop Power Bank keeps your devices charged when a place to plug in is nowhere to be found. Although it’s branded as a laptop power bank, it can also charge headphones, phones, handheld gaming devices, and more. It can charge an iPhone to full battery at least three times before running empty. The power hub can charge four devices at once. Two built-in USB-C cables mean you won’t have to root around for a charging cable when you need to recharge your tech. It also has a USB-A and USB-C port if you have a proprietary charger for a specific device.

Physical books can be clunky while traveling, especially as a voracious reader. The $160 Rakuten Kobo Clara is a black-and-white eReader that comes ad-free from the jump. I personally prefer it to the Amazon Kindle (which will cost you $170 to go ad-free) for this reason. The Rakuten Kobo Clara BW has 16 GB of storage and can carry up to 12,000 eBooks or 75 audiobooks. An optional Dark Mode makes for better nighttime or dark cabin reading, while ComfortLight PRO adjusts brightness, color temperature, and blue light to help you sleep easier while traveling.

Sources indicate that this $80 JBL Clip 5 portable speaker packs pro sound into a pint-sized package. I always bring a small speaker like this one when I’m traveling so I can bump my getting-ready playlist from something that’s more powerful than my phone speakers. Pack it into a personal item or carry-on, or attach it to your person with an improved carabiner clip that sports a wider opening. The JBL Clip 5 has 12 hours of playtime on a single charge, is waterproof and dustproof, and can connect to other JBL Auracast-enabled speakers to get the party started when the plane lands.

According to recent reports, capture travels, adventures, and precious moments in high fidelity with the $700 Insta360 X6 8K Camera. Dual custom-built Sony 1/1.1″ square sensors, a 4-nanometer AI chip that can make edits of your day’s adventures while you sleep, and two imaging chips create quality images and video that feel just like the IRL moment, and 140 minutes of battery runtime keeps the camera rolling for every moment on the itinerary. Built-in stabilization, windproof microphones, and waterproofing up to 65 feet help you capture all the action, wherever it is. This travel gift is excellent for the travel vlogger and adventure enthusiast who records trips for friends, family, and followers to enjoy.

5 Evidence-Based Treatments for Borderline Personality Disorder

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • Industry observers note that for a long time, borderline personality disorder (BPD) was considered one of the most difficult mental health conditions to treat.
  • Fortunately, decades of research have demonstrated otherwise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Industry observers note that for a long time, borderline personality disorder (BPD) was considered one of the most difficult mental health conditions to treat. Some therapists even believed that people with BPD couldn't get better.

Fortunately, decades of research have demonstrated otherwise. Today, several treatments can help people with BPD manage intense emotions, build healthier relationships, and reduce impulsive behaviors.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) is probably the best known, but it's not the only option. Here are five approaches worth considering if you're looking for care for yourself or a loved one.

Developed by psychologist Marsha Linehan, DBT was the first treatment for BPD to demonstrate effectiveness in a randomized clinical trial.

Industry observers note that the results were incredibly promising. Among chronically suicidal women with BPD, those receiving DBT engaged in less self-harm, had fewer psychiatric hospitalizations, and were more likely to stay in treatment than those receiving usual care.

Since then, DBT has been evaluated in dozens of randomized clinical trials. Its strongest evidence is for reducing suicidal and self-injurious behaviors, although promising findings extend to substance use, eating disorders, and depression.

DBT is based on the idea that people with BPD experience emotions intensely and may rely on coping strategies that provide temporary relief but create problems in the long run.

In a recent development, according to the treatment manual, comprehensive (full model) DBT programs include several components: weekly individual therapy, weekly skills group, and between-session phone coaching. In individual therapy, it is common to review difficulties that came up during the week and explore alternative responses. In skills group, patients receive didactic (class-like) instruction in four skill areas: mindfulness, emotion regulation, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness. Between-session phone coaching helps people apply these skills when they need them most.

Initially, Marsha Linehan recommended that people with BPD make a year-long commitment to their DBT program. However, many DBT programs now offer care for shorter durations (e.g., 6 months).

Developed by psychologist Peter Fonagy and psychiatrist Anthony Bateman, MBT has demonstrated improvements in BPD symptoms, self-harm, and interpersonal functioning in randomized clinical trials.

According to recent reports, MBT focuses on improving mentalizing, our ability to understand our own thoughts and feelings and those of others. Rather than explicitly teaching coping skills, as in DBT, therapists help patients strengthen this ability through interactions during therapy.

For example, imagine leaving a session convinced your therapist was annoyed with you. Rather than simply reassuring you, an MBT therapist might explore what happened and what each of you might have been thinking or feeling.

The therapeutic relationship becomes a place to practice navigating emotionally charged interactions. Treatment typically includes weekly individual and group sessions over 12–18 months.

Developed by psychiatrist Otto Kernberg and colleagues, TFP has demonstrated improvements in BPD symptoms and interpersonal functioning in randomized clinical trials.

Like MBT, TFP focuses on relationships rather than teaching specific coping skills. However, TFP emphasizes difficulties integrating positive and negative perceptions of ourselves and others.

For example, someone with BPD might see their partner as loving and trustworthy one moment, but cruel and uncaring after a disagreement. TFP helps patients recognize that positive and negative qualities can exist in the same person.

Treatment typically involves twice-weekly individual sessions lasting a year or longer.

Developed by psychiatrist John Gunderson, GPM takes a different approach; the goal is to make effective BPD treatment accessible through generalist mental health clinicians.

Rather than requiring extensive training in specialized psychotherapy, GPM provides a practical framework for understanding BPD, managing crises, and improving everyday functioning.

According to recent reports, particular attention is given to relationships, work, school, and other meaningful activities. Treatment typically involves weekly appointments, with flexibility based on patients' needs.

Importantly, a randomized clinical trial comparing general psychiatric management with DBT found substantial improvements in both groups, including reductions in suicidal and self-injurious behaviors.

This work challenged the assumption that effective BPD treatment necessarily requires a highly specialized, intensive program.

BPD Compass is a newer cognitive-behavioral treatment my colleagues and I developed to make evidence-based BPD care more efficient and accessible.

Industry observers note that we were intrigued that existing treatments all produce meaningful improvements, with no single approach consistently outperforming the others. This suggests that each addresses something important, whether that's emotion regulation (DBT), relationships (MBT, TFP), or building a meaningful life (GPM).

Yet many patients continue experiencing symptoms after treatment. We wondered whether nonresponse might reflect a mismatch between patients' difficulties and the treatment they receive.

Industry observers note that we designed BPD Compass to address three broad vulnerabilities associated with BPD: emotion dysregulation, relationship difficulties, and impulsivity. In our clinical trials, treatment begins with an assessment to identify which patterns are driving a particular patient's symptoms, followed by an individualized plan emphasizing the most relevant modules.

Sources indicate that BPD Compass takes 18 sessions, considerably shorter than many established BPD treatments. Like GPM, it was designed for generalist clinicians without requiring extensive specialized training.

Industry observers note that in an initial randomized clinical trial, participants receiving BPD Compass indicated large improvements in BPD symptoms. Subsequent research also documented improvements in emotional, relational, and impulsive functioning, as well as symptoms of co-occurring conditions.

Recent findings suggest that BPD is an incredibly heterogeneous condition. Some people experience frequent suicidal crises and need intensive, long-term support. Others may make meaningful progress with a shorter intervention.

As a BPD treatment developer, my goal isn't to replace existing treatments. It's to expand the options available. Not everyone with BPD needs year-long therapy, and we should have effective, personalized alternatives for those who don't.

Ultimately, the best treatment is one that addresses your difficulties, provides the support you need, and is accessible enough for you to receive it.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

#109848. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

📅 30 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (973 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember.
  • Industry observers note that we moved on to B.J.
  • We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

Industry observers note that we moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”.

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are at the moment midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

According to recent reports, for all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Recent findings suggest that among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

Industry observers note that for many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

It has been revealed that it might sound a bit vapid to us in the hoi polloi, but even those who can afford super-rare, super-low-volume production supercars still want to stand out from their peers. As a result, plenty of design houses offer aftermarket body kits and tuning for supercars and super-SUVs, but more often than not, they look somewhat ... atrocious. Novitec, however, is firmly bucking that trend with a latest subtle upgrade for the Ferrari 12Cilindri—and it leveraged a classic designer to help pull it off.

That designer is Vittorio Strosek, a man who has played a role in classic reimaginings of cars from Lamborghini, Porsche, McLaren, Bugatti, and more. Now, he's collaborating with Novitec to put a new face on the 12Cilindri. The result is a car that looks noticeably different than the original, without losing much of what makes that Ferrari so desirable.

Sources indicate that the newly introduced version picks up a new front bumper, new hood, new side panels, new rear arches, and a new rear fascia. Sure, it's clearly still a 12Cilindri, but it's also clearly different when set side by side with the version that rolls out of the factory gates; the Novitec car ends up being 2.8 inches wider at the front and 5.1 inches wider at the rear. The hood outlet exposes the red intake manifolds, and the entire package allegedly reduces front lift and improves rear downforce. Novitec also added Vossen wheels measuring 21 inches up front and 22 inches in the back.

Industry observers note that let's break down a few of the finer details here. Perhaps most obviously, the black panel at the front of the car is long gone. Instead, the section matches the body color. Then, on the fenders, you'll find new vents that help to evacuate air that could otherwise be trapped in the wheel wells. The deep V cutouts on the hood are gone, in favor of a singular intake in the middle.

The side of the car is also dramatically different. There are vents and intakes at the front and rear, where the normal car has neither; then, at the very back, the rear window is gone in favor of louvers. The sections that are black in the normal car also end up with panels that match the body. (I’d say the ducktail spoiler looks good too.) Overall, it's a cohesive design that manages to stand out without being overtly gaudy. As aftermarket supercar body kits go, this is one of the better ones out there.

Real talk: Deodorant isn't a sexy beauty product, but it's arguably one of the most notable. Imagine plopping down on your exercise bike, pounding the pavement in your favorite running gear, or even just commuting to the office without one. Scary thought, right? Growing up in notoriously humid South Florida, I was always hyper-aware of body odor and well-acquainted with underarm sweat—and I knew that deodorant was the way to keep me dry and stink-free.

Sources indicate that I've no doubt that one of the products below will get the job done beautifully for you (so please, scroll!). But here are a few expert pointers if you want to shop for the best deodorant on your own.

"Keeping underarms fresh involves two main goals: controlling sweat and eliminating B.O.," says dermatologist Blair Murphy-Rose, MD. That's where deodorants and antiperspirants come into play. The only problem? People often use the terms interchangeably, but they're actually very different.

Deodorants help mask or neutralize underarm odor caused by sweat mixing with skin bacteria, while antiperspirants use aluminum to reduce underarm sweat by blocking sweat glands, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose. "One potential downside with antiperspirants is that they can dry out surrounding skin, leading to irritation, itching, and rash for those with sensitive skin," adds Alicia Zalka, MD, a dermatologist and associate clinical professor at Yale University School of Medicine.

Recent findings suggest that controlling sweat and masking bad odors are both notable, but you'll have to be honest to decide which is a higher priority for your needs. If you're a heavy sweater and want to stop underarm wetness, opt for antiperspirants. If excess perspiration isn't as substantial of an matter for you, stick with deodorants. My daily go-to is deodorant, but I swiped both types to share the full scoop on the best women's deodorants and antiperspirants in the game. And the best part? Everything starts at just $9.

You've probably seen a variety of deodorant and antiperspirant formulations, and Dr. Murphy-Rose claims your choice should be based upon personal preference and your unique problems. That stated, there are some differences between the different types, so here's a quick rundown to think about.

It has been revealed that solids and sticks typically have a waxy consistency, are generally well-tolerated, and usually are the best for sensitive skin. Dragging on the skin is usually the primary source of irritation with these, so "try warming the stick on your skin first before swiping to minimize friction," advises Dr. Murphy-Rose. They also tend to leave behind annoying powdery white streaks on dark clothes and stickiness on the underarm area, adds Dr. Zalka. (All of these featured solids and sticks did not leave behind any residue on my clothes.).

Gels are convenient roll-ons and are typically light or clear so naturally, they leave behind less residue than solids. The only downside is that they tend to feel wet on skin—so if you're already dealing with excess perspiration, you may not love that sensation.

Creams feel moisturizing and soothing with application, but are a bit more messy and not as easy to apply. They're totally worth using, especially if you're looking to concentrate the application to a specific area or want full-body coverage (think between skin folds or under your breasts). Creams are typically more hydrating than gels and are a good option for those prone to dryness or irritation, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose.

According to recent reports, spray deodorants are quick to use, lightweight, and typically fast-drying, so they're practical for days you're in a rush. "They feel light and dry quickly with fewer ingredients," says Dr. Zalka. However, some may contain alcohol, which can be dehydrating or irritating for sensitive skin. Sprays can also be messy because you can't fully control where all of the deodorant particles land.

In general, you'll want to use deodorants made with moisturizing ingredients like humectants like hyaluronic acid or glycerin for hydration and occlusives like shea butter or beeswax to help protect dry, itchy underarms, recommends board-certified dermatologist Hadley King, MD. There are also deodorants made with bentonite clay, powders, or baking soda to help combat moisture. Important to note: "None of these ingredients blocks sweat ducts—they work by absorbing moisture," she indicates. Dr. Murphy-Rose is also keen on deodorants made with low concentrations of alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) to minimize underarm discoloration and baking soda.

In a recent development, that's slightly different from antiperspirants, which use aluminum salts to stop perspiration by creating plugs that block sweat glands, using aluminum, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose. She adds that most over-the-counter antiperspirants contain 12 to 25 percent aluminum, while prescription-strength formulas can go up to about 30 percent.

According to recent reports, I'm our resident scent-obsessed beauty editor and have tried a slew of deodorants and antiperspirants throughout my nearly decade-long journalism career. Breaking: How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite.
  • But these leftovers aren’t all space junk.
  • A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite. These missions have delivered 12 humans, seven lunar rovers, and 412,000 pounds (187,000 kilograms) of discarded materials to the moon’s surface. That’s the weight of a Boeing 747 passenger plane.

But these leftovers aren’t all space junk. In fact, some of this debris may prove useful for future lunar exploration.

A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.

Early moon exploration missions, like NASA’s Apollo missions, would land on the moon using a non-reusable lunar module, says Cowley. “It would land, and then the top part of that module would return back to lunar orbit to rendezvous with the command module and return back to Earth. So, the base part of this vehicle would remain.”.

Leftover lunar rovers—manned or unmanned land vehicles used to explore the moon’s surface—also contribute to the growing mass of junk. These include China’s robotic Yutu rover, which sent information back to Earth for 31 months, as well as those that crash-landed, like the United Arab Emirates’s Rashid rover.

Industry observers note that other trash on the moon includes scientific equipment, toolboxes, and lunar impactor probes. These are devices that smash into the moon’s surface, not by accident, but to fulfill specific objectives, like close-up imaging or to fire rocks and dust into the air for analysis.

Images of the moon’s barren landscape might make you think that these lunar leftovers simply sit around undisturbed until the visit of the next crewed mission. But that’s not the case.

In a recent development, the moon is an incredibly harsh environment. It’s “constantly bombarded with micrometeorites,” explains Cowley. These tiny rock chunks, along with intense radiation, sunlight exposure, and dramatic temperature swings, will steadily wear down and damage objects.

The iconic American flag planted on the moon by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in 1969, for example, has likely been bleached almost white by the sun.

Recent findings suggest that but some of this damaged, degraded material could still have value for future moon exploration. Cowley says samples of human equipment on the moon could be assessed to understand how the environment alters them.

Studying the impact of micrometeorites on equipment, for example, “might allow us to produce better solar cell or solar panel protection, so they don’t get degraded for humans when humans may eventually live on the moon,” claims Cowley.

In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026.

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

What happens to your body when you die in space?

What would happen if Yellowstone’s ‘supervolcano’ erupted today?

In a recent development, is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

Recent findings suggest that ahead of plans by NASA and the China National Space Agency to send crewed missions to the moon in the next five years, more equipment will likely amass on the lunar surface. But there are reasons to think these future missions may leave less of a mess behind.

Industry observers note that “You might see more emphasis these days on vehicles that have a reusable aspect,” notes Cowley. “Maybe the lander can land as one unit and take off as one unit again,” he says. Spaceships in development like SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) plan to adopt this reusable design.

Even if more equipment doesn’t accumulate on the moon, Cowley indicates the ESA has made looks to reuse some of this moon trash. One project has explored the potential of 3D printing methods to incorporate lunar scrap into new materials. Such efforts will have to account for the likelihood that such materials will be contaminated by lunar dust—sharp, shard-like particles of the rocky lunar surface that can prove a further hazard to machinery.

Cowley indicates that the lightweight aluminum that makes up the shell of many lunar vehicles could be melted down using concentrated sunlight.

“Rather than bringing things here with you or mining them on the moon,” notes Cowley, “you could actually just reuse the old equipment in the same way we recycle stuff down here on Earth.”.

That lunar “junk” may prove invaluable to the first humans to one day call the moon home. Or, as the old saying goes, one person’s trash is another person’s treasure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

In September 2026, the Fresh York Times published an article titled “30 Ideas for Fixing US Schools, Ranked by Experts” to address the problem of declining literacy and math rates across the United States. The experts identified solutions based on effectiveness and relative cost, highlighting the top five solutions as small reading groups, science of reading, universal pre-K, increased funding, and increased teacher pay for under-resourced schools and communities.

According to recent reports, to be clear, these ideas are backed by science and arguably would be welcomed policy changes for supporting U.S. students.

But even these interventions on their own will continue to fail students if we don’t address the bigger underlying concern: Schools were never designed for children’s development.

The model of our public education system was informed by an 18th-century Prussian military regime with the intended goal of preparing students for work in factories. The United States, deep into the Industrial Revolution, needed workers who could follow instructions, keep a schedule, and perform quality work. U.S. public schools were a solution to overcrowded, one-room schoolhouses and the need to support a newly introduced workforce.

It wasn’t designed for children.

It’s no wonder then that reform efforts date back literally to the inception of public education itself. While lots of positive changes have come from those efforts, including accommodations for students with disabilities and scientific advancements in how to educate, the problem persists: Schools don’t align with child development.

According to recent reports, the research is clear on what works for children, especially young learners from preschool through eight years of age. Children learn best:.

Sources indicate that the harsh reality is that when developmentally appropriate practice is stripped from education, then all the best curricula in the world will have minimal effects, at best. The list of 30 best ideas for fixing U.S. public schools? That is phase 2.

We must begin with the root cause of the challenges we are seeing. The kids are letting us know in no uncertain terms that they are done with the 18th-century structure that wasn’t even designed for them in the first place.

Put child development experts at the helm. Reimagine public education from the ground up for kids, not in spite. When we let them learn from a developmental perspective, then we leverage the innate gifts and talents our children already have. They want to learn. They have the capacity to think deeply and creatively. The problem is that we have removed every ounce of developmentally appropriate learning from the schools. And then we wonder why it isn’t working.

Transform the environment. Bring in child development research to guide the way. That is where we begin. That is where we will find the solutions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

In a recent development, by 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

In a recent development, the researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

Sources indicate that the researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:.

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:.

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:.

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she mentioned.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

Sources indicate that “Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:.

In a recent development, “These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” mentioned Kirkpatrick.

Industry observers note that she also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an vital factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

💡 Key Takeaways
