#109820. 6 Signs Grand Theft Auto VI Is Coming Between You and Your Partner

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1307 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

6 Signs Grand Theft Auto VI Is Coming Between You and Your Partner

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) has finally arrived, and many people are signing off from their lives and signing on to the virtual world.
  • The graphics and attention to detail are remarkably realistic, making the experience immersive, even when painting your virtual bedroom in anticipation of your girlfriend coming home from prison.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) has finally arrived, and many people are signing off from their lives and signing on to the virtual world. Set in the fictional, Florida-inspired state of Leonida, the latest installment takes you through palm-tree-lined streets, lavish estates, neon-lit nightclubs, and alligator-infested swamps. In this world, you can cruise in a sports car listening to a killer soundtrack featuring artists such as Tame Impala, Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott, and PinkPantheress.

The graphics and attention to detail are remarkably realistic, making the experience immersive, even when painting your virtual bedroom in anticipation of your girlfriend coming home from prison.

Industry observers note that in the weeks leading up to the release, it has been intriguing to see how frequently the excitement surrounding this game has made its way into my therapy sessions. So many people have talked about taking time off from work and booking hotel rooms so they can play uninterrupted. Many are considering skipping the holidays this year and spending Thanksgiving in Vice City rather than at the dinner table with their families.

As a couples therapist, I find this idea of disappearing into a virtual world fascinating, and to some extent, understand the appeal. Who wouldn't want to check out right now? Between geopolitical tensions and the threat of AI taking people’s jobs, reality hasn't been doing a great job of selling itself lately.

According to recent reports, entering a world where you don't have to worry about grades, respond to your mother's texts about the holidays, or figure out what to make for dinner while accommodating everyone's increasingly complicated dietary restrictions can be appealing. But when does checking out become a problem for your relationship?

Interestingly, at the center of GTA VI is the story of a couple, Jason and Lucia, who rely on one another to survive. Imagine spending hours navigating the complexities of a fictional couple's relationship while neglecting your own.

It’s remarkable how resourceful we become when we truly want something. Couples regularly tell me they’re too busy and too exhausted to proposal date nights, weekend getaways, or even small, thoughtful gestures. Yet many of those same people somehow find bandwidth to take days off work, book hotel rooms, and clear their schedule for a video game.

According to recent reports, A person may spend six hours tending to their virtual snake and re-stealing a car, but an hour of bedtime for their children feels like a waste of time. In Vice City, they have energy to strategize, learn from their mistakes, and keep trying, but when it comes to being emotionally available for their partner, they're ready to call it a night. Getting their relationship with Lucia from "Running on Empty" to "Hot Together" is worth an entire weekend, but planning an outing with their real partner requires three weeks' notice and a Google Calendar invitation. These are signs that focus on the game is having a negative effect on the real-world relationship.

Recent findings suggest that part of the appeal is that, in the game, the objectives are clear. Real relationships are messier. There are no YouTube tutorials walking you through every challenge or showing you how other people solved it. Still, if you can devote hours to mastering the complexities of repainting your car, finding newly introduced sunglasses, and stashing your weapon, some of that patience and determination can also be made available for the people in your real life.

If your partner is repeatedly calling you for dinner or your children are begging you to come see something they've been building, and these requests feel like inconveniences standing between you and your next engine upgrade, it might be worth examining what's happening.

Fascinating how buying flowers, answering texts, and remembering a girlfriend's preferences can become second nature to a person when a little heart pops up on the screen to celebrate, while managing these things in real life can feel like a difficult challenge.

Sources indicate that it's important to remember that one of our most fundamental attachment needs is knowing that we can reach our partner and that they will respond when we need them (Johnson, 2008). When mundane attempts at connection generate responses of irritation or withdrawal, people will eventually learn to stop reaching out. Maybe initially, the peace and quiet can feel like a victory, but eventually, it will get in the way of what we really want, which is meaningful, loving, and connected relationships.

Recent findings suggest that booking a hotel room to spend three days playing a video game while your spouse drives your kids to soccer practice or plans your family's Thanksgiving meal is not a decision that just concerns you. Being in a committed partnership doesn't require relinquishing your personhood. It does, however, involve recognizing that your choices have consequences for other people.

In a recent development, creating a couple bubble is about establishing a mutual agreement to protect and prioritize the relationship and look out for each other (Tatkin, 2012). It is healthy to want some space for our hobbies in our relationship, but when our leisure comes at our partner's expense, that will hurt the partnership.

According to recent reports, in my practice, I see many couples whose romantic relationships gradually deteriorate into parent-child dynamics. One partner assumes more of the adult responsibilities. They begin monitoring screen time, reminding the other person of their obligations, managing household chores, worrying about their health, keeping track of bedtimes and meals, and making sure someone highlights up to pick up the kids.

Meanwhile, the partner being "parented" feels criticized, controlled, micromanaged, and deprived of their freedom. This is not a healthy dynamic between adult partners.

In a recent development, the most alluring part of an alternate reality is that you can leave your emotional baggage behind. You don't have to process grief, worry about your aging parents, or think about the Christmas gifts you can't afford.

You can avoid difficult conversations about whether you're going to get married or try IVF treatment. And of course, unwinding is important to recovery, but before you know it, you can find yourself looking forward to your partner falling asleep so you can finally enjoy your evening by yourself.

You're working tirelessly to get your relationship with Lucia to "Hot Together" while your actual partner is wondering whether filing for divorce would finally unlock your attention.

Industry observers note that the desire to escape isn't abnormal or shameful. We're overloaded and overstimulated. Real life is difficult, and our sense of agency is constantly challenged. However, it is valuable to understand what exactly it is that we are running away from.

As much as the desire to retreat into a different reality is understandable, we also could make our actual lives different, but of course, making real-life changes requires being present.

None of this means we can't enjoy the art, music, and unapologetically excessive world that GTA offers. But the real challenge isn't completing another mission; it's figuring out how to bring some of that same excitement, curiosity, and determination back into your relationship.

Balan, D. (2023). Re-Write: A Trauma Workbook of Creative Writing and Recovery in Our New Normal. Routledge. https://www.duygubalan.com/re-write.

In a recent development, balan, D., Balan, Y., & Balan, N. (2025). Confidently chill: An anxiety workbook for new adults. Routledge. https://www.duygubalan.com/confidently-chill.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An 83 year old Congressional representative who sent an embarrassing letter to a well-meaning 10 year old constituent on the topic of electric cars and climate change, where she seems to brag about saddling his generation with debt through a recent climate rollback she voted for, is presently losing her seat.

Sources indicate that upgrade: This article was originally posted on May 14, but we wanted to update it with news of the election result. As of now, with 100% of votes counted, Foxx is losing by 362 votes, but has requested a recount. We’re updating this article with the most current information on the race below.

Sources indicate that christian Mango is ten years old, and was encouraged by his elementary school class to write a letter about a topic of his choice, and mail it to a decisionmaker. Christian chose his Congressional representative, 83 year old Virginia Foxx.

Recent findings suggest that foxx is an 11-term Congresswoman in North Carolina, one of the most gerrymandered states in the nation, and was expected to win a 12th term in the heavily republican district, having previously proudly touted an endorsement from an enemy of the US who tried to overthrow the government. Her opponent is Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a former journalist and native of the district.

Sources indicate that for the topic of his letter, Christian chose electric cars – which is what makes this story relevant to us here at Electrek. Christian laid out several points about EVs, stating that “they’re better than normal cars. They’re better for the environment. They pay less. And there’s no gas.” (All true! well done Christian).

Christian suggested that electric cars could be incentivized with a $5,000 tax rebate – lower than the $7.5k EVs used to get, but better than the $0 they get federally today (compare to the ~$20k in ignored costs that gas cars still benefit from).

Christian went on to suggest action on climate change, stating “maybe there is still a chance for 6.5 million people to not die anymore and for the weather to get better just maybe glaciers stop melting.” Christian was probably referring to the number of people who die from air pollution globally each year (though several estimates suggest that number is actually higher, and Christian did conflate climate and weather… but we’ll give him a pass on this one, his heart is in the right place).

Sources indicate that christian was proud of his letter, as was his mother, Emily Mango, who stated “he researched, cited facts, and made good arguments in his essay – an essay that had nothing to do with politics. He was proud of his essay.”.

But then he got a response, and that’s when things took a turn for the worse. Christian’s mother Emily angrily shared the response on Instagram, where it gained traction.

Emily said Foxx’s screed was “disrespectful, hostile and unkind” and called it “demoralizing and reprehensible.” She said she had to speak to her son and teach him that this response was “not okay,” and that “nobody should talk to a child like that and nobody should talk to a teacher like that.”.

I’d also add that it’s full of disinformation, and that it even seems to brag about the massive debt that Foxx has imposed on Christian’s generation.

According to recent reports, foxx includes six links, all from propaganda publications that deny the science of climate change. 3 are from from WSJ (2 of which are opinion pieces) and 1 is from Fox, both of which are owned by the same climate denier, Rupert Murdoch. 1 is from Washington Times, a tabloid founded by a religious cult (yes, really), and 1 is from another right-wing climate denying publication, National Review.

Notably, none of the six links have anything to do with electric cars.

In the text of the response, Foxx touts republicans’ “all of the above” energy policy, which is ironic given that the party whose energy policy she touts has spent most of the last year forcing broken dirty coal plants open (which they are still doing after ruled illegal) and trying to shut down clean cheap ones. Apparently “all of the above” is code for “fossil fuels and nothing else.”.

It has been revealed that foxx’s letter does not directly address the strengths of electric cars, despite them being the subject of Christian’s letter. Notably, EVs actually can receive energy from any generation method, whether it be wind, solar, or even coal or gas – whereas gas-powered vehicles can only use one type of energy, oil. Thus, an “all of the above” strategy should probably find EVs the preferable route for transportation.

But in apparent contradiction to Foxx’s surely sincerely held belief that we should pursue an “all of the above” energy policy – which electric cars would help to achieve – she in fact has voted against EVs when given the opportunity.

Foxx claims in her response that she can’t support tax credits on electric cars, because those go to “mostly people with higher incomes who are able to purchase ‘fresh’ electric cars.”.

According to recent reports, but she in fact voted against, and later voted to repeal, incentives which were limited to lower-income-earners and were only available on cars up to a certain MSRP cap. Further, they were available on used vehicles, not just latest ones – suggesting that Foxx doesn’t know what she voted against.

Foxx was one of 218 republicans to vote in favor of a ~$4 trillion giveaway to wealthy elites. Her vote raised electric bills and threatened US energy security and surrendered US manufacturing jobs to China. Some of the money given away to wealthy elites in the bill was clawed back from energy efficiency programs that had been going to regular Americans.

In a recent development, those energy efficiency programs had been instituted by the Inflation Reduction Act, the Biden-era law which established tax credits for EVs and other efficiency rebates. The Inflation Reduction Act was actually revenue positive, which is to say it reduced the national debt (by $238B), rather than adding to it, because of provisions to increase enforcement against wealthy tax cheats.

But most of the IRA was repealed by the bill that Foxx voted for, meaning the US lost out on those deficit reductions. All in all, the bill Foxx voted for would add $4 trillion to the national debt – which, incidentally, is another point Foxx touches on in her response.

In one sentence, she seems to directly mock Christian, telling him that “YOU and your classmates will be responsible for that debt” as part of a warning about the dangers of government debt.

Recent findings suggest that but I read this sentence as mockery, rather than as a sincere warning, given that Foxx voted to add $4 trillion to the national debt, which she, at 83 years old, knows she will not have to pay off. Christian, who is 10, will likely spend his whole life saddled with the debt Foxx voted for.

According to recent reports, he will also have to pay for her inaction on climate change, which will have increasingly worse effects on the world Christian will grow up into. Foxx’s generation has already felt the heat, with the massive floods that devastated her state in 2024, from a hurricane that was made 200x more likely due to climate change. Now, imagine how much worse it could get if Foxx’s policies remained in place until 72 years from now when Christian will be her age.

Foxx then closes out the letter with disparaging remarks about teachers, claiming that they are “too interested in indoctrinating you,” and warning Christian about “propaganda.” Which I guess shows where Foxx’s attitude comes from – if she has spent her 83 years never trusting anyone who knows more than her about a topic, that would certainly lead to the ignorance reflected in her letter.

Foxx – who somehow has a doctorate in education and right now sits on the Congressional education committee – could have turned this into a nice moment to teach the child who wrote her something about democracy and responsive government, but instead turned it into a moment to teach the world what’s wrong with her.

When we first wrote this article, Foxx had a projected 97% chance of winning in a district which voted for her by a 19% margin in 2024.

But that was before America (and its short memory) was reminded of how incapable republicans are of leading anything.

Sources indicate that after a pile of economic crises caused by Donald Trump’s incompetent “leadership,” and his continued participation in an 8-month-and-counting war of choice that is spiking energy prices worldwide, bringing oil profits to record highs (and attempting to distract the news from talking about the Epstein files, which he is heavily featured in and has tried to cover up), America was once again fed up. And his incompetence took his entire party down with him.

Safe republican seats were flipped around the country in the biggest “wave” election we’ve seen in recent times, with the Democrats gaining control of both the House and Senate.

And it looks like Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a Wilkes county native and former journalist, who also ran against Foxx in 2024, will now get his chance to represent the people of North Carolina’s 5th district… assuming a recount goes in his favor.

The situation in North Carolina is particularly interesting, given that republicans had done an emergency redraw of district lines in an attempt to cheat their way to winning more seats.

Generally, district lines get redrawn after each Census, which happens on the decade mark, rather than mid-decade. But republicans saw ahead of time that they were likely to lose the House due to their unpopularity, and wanted to fudge the numbers in several states instead of going for a fair fight.

Foxx’s main argument against Christian’s suggested $5,000 EV incentive, is increasing national debt. Yet in just one tax bill, her approval increases the national debt over 10%. This is not Christian’s “responsibility”, this burden is forced on him, along with climate change.

Industry observers note that so they engaged in Gerrymandering, a process wherein district lines are redrawn to favor a particular political party. The idea is to put as many of your opponents’ votes into a few safe seats as possible, while spreading out your own votes to a wider range of seats that you win each by a small margin.

But it turns out that republicans were even more unpopular than they thought, and as a result, their Gerrymandering backfired. Those narrow margins they sought ended up flipping more seats than would have otherwise flipped, turning North Carolina almost completely blue in what analysts have called a “Dummymander“. (NC-5 itself was not one of the redrawn districts, though – it just swung 19 whole points to the Dems).

That mentioned: the race is not over yet. The deadline to request a recount is today, and sure enough, Foxx has done so. The current margin is extremely thin, just 0.12% of votes, so things could certainly change in a recount. Foxx also vowed to run again in 2028, hoping for a less hostile political environment. She will be 85 years old at the time of that election.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • BMW officially opened its newly introduced Plant Woodruff in South Carolina on November 13, marking the start of series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) electric vehicle batteries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iX5 is BMW’s first fully electric vehicle built in the US, promising an estimated up to 456 miles of range, ultra-fast charging speeds, and plenty of Neue Klasse tech.

BMW officially opened its newly introduced Plant Woodruff in South Carolina on November 13, marking the start of series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) electric vehicle batteries.

The Gen6 batteries will power BMW’s upcoming “X” electric vehicles, starting with the all-new iX5 SUV.

The iX5 is being built about 15 miles away at BMW Group Plant Spartanburg, the company’s first fully electric model to be assembled in the US.

BMW Plant Spartanburg is churning out around 70 iX5s a day following a $1.7 billion investment in South Carolina to expand the plant for EV production and build the upcoming battery assembly plant in Woodruff.

According to Robert Engelhorn, president and CEO of BMW Manufacturing in Spartanburg, the manufacturer is confident the iX5 will attract buyers, promising 435 miles of range, ultra-fast charging, and its updated Neue Klasse technology and design.

Engelhorn told Automotive News in an interview that “there’s a clear trend globally for EVs,” adding that “We will contribute to this growth from the BMW side.”.

BMW didn’t provide a specific production estimate for the iX5, but suppliers were reportedly told it would be around 60,000 EVs in 2027, down from 100,000 it initially forecasted.

“We said we would begin assembling fully electric BMW vehicles in the US by the end of 2026 – and we are delivering on that commitment,” Engelhorn said.

A manufacturer spokesperson confirmed that the iX5 will initially use battery cells from China before switching to US-sourced cells from LG Energy Solutions plant in Arizona by the end of the decade.

With production now underway, the iX5 is expected to begin arriving at US dealerships in early 2027.

In a recent development, the 2027 BMW iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800. BMW estimates the 144 kWh battery will provide up to 456 miles of range, up from the 435 miles it previously estimated.

It features BMW’s fresh “double-X” light signature, which combines the headlights, daytime running lights, side lights, and turn signals into one unit. The Double-X headlights come standard, but BMW remarked you can switch them for simpler diagonal stripes.

Last month, BMW showcased the i5’s ultra-fast-charging capabilities during a media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic.

During the demo, the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW, which BMW said enables it to add an impressive up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes.

The electric SUV features a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain setup that delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque. BMW states it can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds and tow up to 6,000 lbs.

It has been revealed that inside, the iX5 adopts BMW’s Neue Klasse design and tech, like the smaller iX3 SUV. The setup includes a new 17.9″ infotainment touchscreen and BMW’s Panoramic Vision, which spans the bottom of the windshield. There’s also an optional 14.6″ passenger screen for a third display.

This is at the top of our short list. Out of Spec got 411 miles at 70 mph (by contrast the Gravity rated at 450 got 368 on the same run and the R1S rated at 410 got 349). It is a real 400+ mile vehicle with an ability to charge a real 300 miles in ~20 minutes.

It has been revealed that edit: OOS was with 22" wheels rated at 426. It should get >430 with the standard 21" wheels.

Measuring 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, BMW’s latest iX5 is about the size of the Porsche Cayenne Electric.

By 2030, BMW intends to be assembling at least fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg. “This marks the beginning of the next chapter in the success story of the largest plant in our global production network,” Raymond Wittman, BMW’s head of production, said.

Following Debrecen (Hungary), Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Germany), and Shenyang (China), Woodruff is the fourth site in BMW’s production network to begin series production of the Gen6 batteries.

#109812. How Long Should We Wait for Sex, Cohabitation, and Marriage?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (960 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

How Long Should We Wait for Sex, Cohabitation, and Marriage?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • "Wise men say, 'Only fools rush in,' but I can't help falling in love with you." — Elvis Presley.
  • Industry observers note that how long should you wait before having sex?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

"Wise men say, 'Only fools rush in,' but I can't help falling in love with you." — Elvis Presley.

Industry observers note that how long should you wait before having sex? Moving in together? Getting married? These are among the most common questions people ask about romantic relationships. Yet there is no magical timeline that guarantees success. The value of waiting depends on the partners, their circumstances, and the nature of their relationship. Still, one principle often proves valuable: patience.

"Patience is not simply the ability to wait. It's how we behave while we're waiting." — Joyce Meyer.

Industry observers note that there's a crucial distinction between waiting and patience. Waiting is passive: Time passes while little changes. Patience, by contrast, is active. It involves investing in the relationship while recognizing that some developments should not be rushed. Patience creates the conditions for intimacy, trust, and commitment to deepen naturally. Unlike procrastination, which unnecessarily delays action, patience reflects wise timing. The notable question is not how long we wait, but whether we practice patience rather than merely let time pass (Ben‐Ze'ev, 2019; and here).

"I don't have a set time frame for sex, but it's always before it gets super serious. I've got to test-drive the car before buying it." — A woman.

"My boyfriend and I had sex on the first date, and we're still together a year later and talking about getting engaged soon. The right person isn't going to think less of you because of the speedy sex." — A woman.

It has been revealed that sexual attraction is a defining feature of romantic love, making the timing of sexual intimacy especially significant. Research often finds that couples who delay sex report greater relationship quality and lower breakup rates. Waiting may allow emotional intimacy and communication to develop before physical intimacy takes center stage. Some studies suggest that couples who wait several months before becoming sexually involved report greater satisfaction and relationship stability (Vancour & Fallon, 2017).

According to recent reports, yet these findings do not mean that sex on the first date is a mistake. What matters most is not the calendar but the context. Partners differ in their values, attachment styles, and goals. For some well-matched couples, early sexual intimacy may strengthen their initial bond. The key question is therefore not, "How many dates should we wait?" but "Are we both comfortable with the pace at which intimacy is developing?".

"With love and patience, nothing is impossible." — Daisaku Ikeda.

In a recent development, premarital cohabitation has become the norm for most American couples. Yet living together can serve very different purposes.

In a recent development, research suggests that couples who move in together mainly to "test" the relationship are more likely to break up than those who cohabit because they genuinely want to spend more time together (Chapman et al., 2026). One reason is that living together creates practical and financial interdependence, making it harder to evaluate the relationship objectively. Couples who move in together after discussing long-term aims, or after becoming engaged, generally report better marital outcomes than those who simply drift into cohabitation because it feels convenient.

Researchers therefore distinguish between sliding into cohabitation and deciding to cohabit. Sliding involves little deliberate discussion or commitment; deciding reflects conscious consideration of the relationship's future. Indeed, more than half of cohabiting couples report that they had not explicitly discussed moving in together before doing so. The central issue is not whether couples should live together before marriage, but whether cohabitation expresses mutual commitment and thoughtful deliberation rather than uncertainty and inertia.

Industry observers note that "The ideal amount of time to date before getting married is at least a whole year. It's crazy to marry someone before you've seen what they're like in winter." — A woman.

Industry observers note that no dating duration can guarantee marital success. Nevertheless, many relationship researchers and therapists suggest that two to three years often provides enough time to know a partner across different circumstances while preserving romantic momentum.

Dating typically differs from hooking up because it is part of a broader process of building an enduring relationship. Yet the distinction is far from absolute. Many successful relationships begin as casual encounters. One-night stands sometimes become lifelong partnerships, and dating apps such as Tinder, often criticized for promoting casual sex, have also become crucial pathways to marriage. The route matters less than what develops along the way.

"Lovers are patient and know that the moon needs time to become full." — Rumi.

Love has no universally correct timetable. There are no strict rules governing when to have sex, how long to live together, or how long to date before marriage. What matters is not simply how long partners wait before taking the next step, but whether they use that time wisely. Passive waiting merely allows the clock to advance; active patience allows intimacy, trust, and commitment to deepen. Romantic flourishing depends less on the passage of time than on what partners do with it.

Ben-Ze’ev, A. (2019). The Arc of Love: How our romantic lives change over time. University of Chicago Press.

In a recent development, chapman, C. L., Liu, D. Y., Stanley, S. M., & Rhoades, G. K. (2026). Thinking about moving in together? Reasons for cohabitation are associated with relationship outcomes over time. Couple and Family Psychology: Research and Practice, 15, 138-151.

It has been revealed that vancour, J. M., & Fallon, M. (2017). Romantic satisfaction in young adults as a function of sexual debut. Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research, 22(2).‏.

Tech Report: Peeping woodcocks are evolutionary oddballs

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet.
  • Recent findings suggest that woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances.
  • “The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, stated in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet. You’ve probably seen at least a few videos of the birds on social media darting across beaches and being incredibly vocal. As if their small, squat bodies and comically long beaks weren’t enough, they also vocalize with distinctively cartoonish peeping tweets during their mating displays.

Recent findings suggest that woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances. Six of the eight species are only found on specific islands, and some of them don’t even migrate at all. So how did these evolutionary oddballs even get their start—and stop migrating? To piece together their unique avian story, biologists analyzed the DNA of all eight woodcock species and 22 species of snipe.

“The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, stated in a statement. “They’re not terribly aerodynamic, and yet they’ve clearly gotten around.”.

Bates and his colleagues published the results of their work today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). The years-long endeavor involved not only examining preserved woodcock specimens housed in the Field Museum, but a fossilized sandpiper previously excavated from a cave site in Haiti. The remains found on the island of Hispaniola are around 1,000 years old, but that is still extremely young in the grand history of shorebirds.

Industry observers note that the earliest members of the sandpiper family began in the northern hemisphere before slowly migrating to islands along lower latitudes. Those birds subsequently migrated much shorter distances after settling in the warmer climates. However, they didn’t remain sedentary. Based on the DNA analysis detailed in their study, Bates and his team theorize that snipes from Africa eventually traveled across the Atlantic Ocean, then evolved into new species in South America. From there, more of the birds made their way over the Pacific Ocean to New Zealand.

Their examinations also cleared up a bit of confusion. Biologists initially believed the fossilized sandpiper from Haiti was a woodcock, but the most recent data now demonstrates that it’s a snipe.

“Snipes and woodcocks have been around for 20 to 25 million years,” Bates explained. “Over that time, as newly introduced species have evolved and moved around the world, their migratory patterns have changed, too.”.

These changes are likely to continue amid today’s dramatic climate shifts, but that may pose a problem for the beloved woodcocks.

According to recent reports, “These are definitely birds that would be affected by changing habitats and changing climates,” stated Bates. “Some of these woodcocks are found only in the mountain forests on islands between Asia and Australia, and if those forests get cut down, the birds are going to be gone too.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to fresh research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

Sources indicate that the findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, said Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she mentioned.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz said the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

Recent findings suggest that she said researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”.

Weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he noted. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy remarked.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy said. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

In a recent development, wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, debuted in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

The study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also said the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham mentioned adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive proposal,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:.

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

Latest Update: The Electric BMW M3 Delivers Thrills, Synthesized Sounds, and Pretend Gears

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that attend an event organized by BMW’s M Division, and you know what you are going to get.
  • In a recent development, but then, as the noise grew louder, the narrative shifted.
  • We’ve known for some time that the BMW M3 was going to make the switch to becoming an EV, but the reality of what that entails for those watching from outside the car was still a mild shock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that attend an event organized by BMW’s M Division, and you know what you are going to get. Such as plentiful M branding everywhere. It was no surprise when I arrived at BMW’s proving ground in Miramar, France, to experience the M3 prototype for the first time to see numerous flags and banners with the famous slant “M” logo. And it felt equally natural for a moment to be listening to the sound of a hard-worked engine on the test track, with what seemed the entirely M-appropriate howl of a straight-six exhaling through a minimally muffled exhaust.

In a recent development, but then, as the noise grew louder, the narrative shifted. Because it was an M4 GT4 making the compelling racket. The two M3 prototypes that followed it wearing a vibrant, dazzle pattern disguise, were traveling every bit as rapidly but almost entirely silently.

We’ve known for some time that the BMW M3 was going to make the switch to becoming an EV, but the reality of what that entails for those watching from outside the car was still a mild shock. The good news for anyone unsure about such a radical departure for the subbrand is that work on a gasoline-powered M3 is continuing in parallel. The combustion version, with the development code G85, is likely to feature another version of the S58 turbocharged inline-six from the current G80 generation, likely working in conjunction with some level of hybrid assistance. That will be a much more traditional take on the junior M car, but it almost certainly won’t be as powerful or as quick as the fully electric version.

But is our world ready for this level of different?

Recent findings suggest that my first experience at Miramar was a passenger ride around the handling track, sitting in the left seat of one of the four colorfully-wrapped prototypes beside Sven Esch, M’s head of vehicle dynamics. I knew the car had a quad-motor powertrain, with one motor driving each wheel, and I could see it was riding on upcoming Michelin Pilot Sport S 6 tires, but that was about all I had to go on when Esch executed a full launch-control start, one brutal enough to leave me confident the finished car will be another member of the two-second club when it comes to 0–60 times. The other disclosure, delivered from the changing tone of the noise coming from the speakers and the sight of Esch’s fingers working paddles behind the steering wheel, is that BMW is joining Hyundai, Porsche, and Mercedes in having a simulated gear system. The lap also revealed a handling balance familiar from many generations of M cars, with varying angles of oversteer through most of the corners.

There are still many unknowns. Although the cars at Miramar were close to production spec, BMW is keeping many details to itself. There are no performance claims yet. And every number given for power, torque, range and charging speed carried an asterisk leading to an “approximately” proviso. The maximum system output was quoted at 838 hp and 885 lb-ft, with the pair of front motors able to deliver up to 643 hp and 398 lb-ft working together, while the larger two in back max out at a claimed 750 hp and 738 lb-ft. Given the way automotive PR typically works, I would be surprised if any of those figures grew any worse before becoming finalized. But they are clearly a way off the 1153-hp AMG GT 63 4-Door, the 1123-hp Lucid Air Sapphire, and the 1019-hp Porsche Taycan Turbo GT.

The M3 EV uses a different battery pack from the regular i3, with a newly introduced cell design and double-sided cooling to enable huge peak flow rates, with this having approximately 100 kWh of usable energy and operating at up to 800 volts. BMW is predicting an EPA range of 300 miles, and peak DC charging speeds will be around 420 kilowatts—slightly higher than the regular i3 and better than the speediest Taycan, but a way off the 600-kW capability of the AMG. More impressive is the ability of the battery pack to reabsorb energy through regeneration, doing this at rates of up to—approximately again—540 kilowatts. So the equivalent of 724 hp, without having to use the carbon-ceramic discs and pads.

Industry observers note that then there are the simulated gears. Although, pedantically, these are not. BMW has decided the mDrive mode allows the selection of what it calls “stages,” of which there are six. The default mode on startup is actually Automatic, in which the car changes between the stages by itself while playing a corresponding soundtrack as it does so, like a true automatic transmission in drive. There is also a paddle mode that gives you the ability to select a stage and also a simulated limiter if you fail to change up in time. It also has a normal EV single-speed drive mode.

Recent findings suggest that beneath the surface, the M3 has been given a substantial structural work over compared with the i3, the M version getting additional reinforcement for suspension subframes and also plates that bolt to the underfloor battery pack front and rear to better integrate this into the car’s structure. There is also a strut brace between the front suspension towers, eliminating the i3’s frunk, plus smaller reinforcement struts within the A-pillars and on the rear towers.

While the M3 might be beaten by rivals on power statistics, it turns tables with the complexity of its powertrain. Having individual motors for each wheel is a segment first, in contrast with the two-motor Taycan Turbo GT and the three-motor AMG GT 4-Door and Lucid Air Sapphire. The lack of any physical connection between the different wheels means all the functions normally handled by differentials and clutch packs have to be done electronically, a hugely complex task for the dynamic control system. But it also brings benefits, most obvious is the ability to vary the torque going to each individual wheel almost instantly, without the response delay of even the fastest-acting mechanical systems. And it can also do this with regeneration, changing the braking effect on each wheel with equal dexterity.

Industry observers note that my chance to experience all this witchcraft was limited to two stints on the Miramar handling track, following the raucous M4 GTS being piloted by works driver Jens Klingmann at a pretty gentle pace, and with Carsten Wolf, vehicle characteristics manager, riding shotgun. Wolf proved to be a pretty laid-back passenger, but I was only able to switch certain dynamic settings.

Industry observers note that while the electric M3’s cabin architecture is very similar to that of the i3 and the upcoming 3-series, the prototype wore a dashboard cover to obscure what I’m told were unfinished screen-layout designs. The car did have an M-specific version of BMW’s Panoramic Vision extra-long gauge cluster, which features a rendered “rev counter” very similar in design to the one in the new M350 xDrive, two graphic bars moving apart. There was also a small set of color-changing shift lights.

It was immediately clear that performance was on another level to the i3 50 I had driven earlier the same day. The M3 felt every bit as quick as the power figures suggested it should, with none of the shortish straights of the handling track being long enough to bring any sense of acceleration beginning to tail off, even as speeds headed well north of 100 mph, and the M4 GT4 was visibly having to work hard to keep a gap. In a straightline fight, I’m certain the EV would have been the faster car, although riding on Pirelli slicks, and having Klingmann at the wheel, gave the car a clear advantage in corners.

The M3’s steering was heavier than the i3 and M350’s and brought a far better sense of connection to the front tires. Unlike some cars with lots of electrical power going through the front axle, the prototype didn’t suffer from any steering corruption, albeit over what was generally a smooth track surface. Even in the softest Comfort mode, the car turned into corners with a keenness that was clearly being helped by applying different levels of regen to each wheel, which then kept it locked to a chosen line.

In a recent development, or at least, it stayed locked until I started to try and get early onto the accelerator. At which point a newly introduced sensation arrived, unexpected in an M3: mild understeer. The control systems were clearly intervening hard in the background; winding off lock brought full fury back immediately. At Wolf’s suggestion, I pressed the steering wheel’s M1 button to shift the drivetrain and chassis to their Sport setting, reducing the front-end push.

But it required the M2 button, which brought the most aggressive Sport Plus settings, and putting the stability control into its half-off MDM mode to unlock the M3’s party spirit and show the side of its personality I’d first experienced from the passenger’s seat, with progressive, easily controllable oversteer.

Plenty of magic was still going on behind the scenes. I noticed that even if I wasn’t quick to apply opposite lock, the prototype would still hold a tidy drift, the dynamic brain carefully metering the torque going to each corner—I was in no doubt that turning the stability management fully off would be a different level of challenge. But, at last, the M3 was feeling like an M3 should.

The wheel-by-wheel regeneration was much more subtle. The i3 already blends electrical and friction braking seamlessly, and the M3 is on a different level, able to use regen to the point of ABS intervention. The left pedal was firm and proportionate, and I had no sense of when one side was handing over to the other. But even under track loadings, most slowing was being done electrically. At the end of my first stint, Wolf, smiling, handed me an infrared temperature reader and invited me to measure the brake temperatures. At the front, the carbon disc was at just 100 degrees Celsius (212 degrees Fahrenheit), way less than I would expect after 10 minutes of track driving in an 800-hp car that weighs around 5000 pounds. The other advantage of the ability to harvest so much energy is a significant improvement to track range; Wolf indicates that for every three laps the car was recuperating enough for another lap at the same pace.

What about the virtual gears? Sorry, the “stages.” These were less convincing. The sounds being piped over the M3’s speakers are loud and engine-like, especially at lower simulated revs, but they grow more otherworldly and sci-fi as the shift lights start to illuminate: I was detecting distinct notes of TIE fighter. M has deliberately taken a different direction from AMG, which has the GT 4-dr doing a full-fledged V-8 impression. BMW’s approach is arguably the more honest one; the M3 isn’t pretending to be something it isn’t.

Sources indicate that but I noticed that the stages also had much less torque modeling than rivals such as Porsche’s E-Shift system in the Taycan, or the pioneering e-Shift in the Hyundai Ioniq 5N, which started this whole game. Beyond the possibility of hitting the M3’s artificial limiter, being in the wrong gear didn’t bring much obvious penalty on track. After a couple of laps of changing with the paddles, I actually went back to Automatic mode, where the virtual gears shift themselves. Which proved that the rising and falling soundtrack does help orientate corner entry speeds. Driving the slow-down lap with both the stepped gears and the speed sound turned off made the M3 prototype suddenly feel like a sensory deprivation chamber.

Sources indicate that what was a very limited first drive was clearly aimed at raising anticipation for the finished car more than answering every dynamic question. It was enough to prove that this M3 is a radical shift from its predecessors. But also to validate BMW’s claim that it is set to be the fastest and most powerful M car yet. The prototype also felt at home on a racetrack in a way that EVs very rarely do, and it has clearly been designed with circuit work in mind. This is a very, very different M3—and I’m glad there will still be a more traditional one. But the electric version still feels worthy of its famous badge.

Juiced Scrambler Mini introduced as a cooler (and safer) e-bike option for teens and parents

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1036 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding an electric bike for a teenager can be surprisingly tricky.
  • The newly launched Juiced Scrambler Mini looks like it could do a pretty good job of threading that needle.
  • The new youth-sized e-bike takes the mini-motorcycle styling of Juiced’s larger Scrambler models and shrinks it down around 16-inch fat tires, creating a bike designed for riders between 4’0″ and 5’3″ (122 to 160 cm).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding an electric bike for a teenager can be surprisingly tricky. Parents generally want something safe, manageable, and from a reputable company. Teenagers, meanwhile, generally want something that doesn’t look like it was picked out by their parents.

The newly launched Juiced Scrambler Mini looks like it could do a pretty good job of threading that needle.

The new youth-sized e-bike takes the mini-motorcycle styling of Juiced’s larger Scrambler models and shrinks it down around 16-inch fat tires, creating a bike designed for riders between 4’0″ and 5’3″ (122 to 160 cm). But perhaps more importantly for parents, Juiced also built in a PIN-protected speed limiter known as Speed Lock that lets adults decide just how fast the bike can go.

According to recent reports, the Scrambler Mini ships set to a 10 mph (16 km/h) Beginner Mode, but its maximum speed can be adjusted anywhere from 1-20 mph (32 km/h) and then locked behind a four-digit PIN. Juiced notes that riders aged 8-12 should not exceed 10 mph, while riders 13 and older can use the bike at speeds up to 20 mph, subject of course to local laws and regulations. In almost every state and jurisdiction though, the bike will fit Class 2 designation for street-legal riding and bike lane operation.

That setup seems like a pretty smart way to approach youth e-bikes. Instead of buying a slow bike that a teenager may quickly outgrow – or handing them a much faster machine before a parent thinks they’re ready – the same bike can essentially grow with the rider (with speed titrated by a parent or guardian).

And from the kid’s perspective, it certainly doesn’t look like a safety-first children’s bike.

The Scrambler Mini gets the same sort of moto-inspired styling that has defined Juiced’s Scrambler lineup, including a long bench seat, dual-crown-style fork, chunky 16 x 4-inch tires, and several appropriately loud color options including Blackberry, Fruit Punch, Blueberry, and Pink Lemonade.

According to recent reports, there’s some decent hardware underneath that styling, too. The rear hub motor is rated at 500W nominal and 1,092W peak with 80 Nm of torque. A removable 48V 10Ah battery using LG cells provides 480Wh of capacity, with Juiced claiming up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Four levels of cadence-based pedal assist are included, as is a right-side thumb throttle.

Industry observers note that the bike also features Talon hydraulic disc brakes with large 180mm rotors front and rear, 50mm of front suspension travel, an integrated backlit LCD, a headlight, and a rear taillight with brake-light functionality. The single-speed bike weighs 59 lb (26.8 kg), has a 27.15-inch seat height, and is rated for up to 275 lb (125 kg) of payload.

Those parts are far above what we normally see on e-bikes targeted towards teens, with most teen-focused e-bikes sporting cheaper components like mechanical brakes and rigid forks.

Industry observers note that the Scrambler Mini is listed at $1,099, though Juiced is currently offering a Black Friday sale that drops the price by another $150 to just $949. The organization notes preorders are expected to begin shipping the week of December 7.

In a recent development, that price also comes with something increasingly vital in the crowded youth e-bike market: an actual company standing behind the bike. Juiced was founded in 2009, quickly becoming a leader in the market for powerful and stylish e-bikes. But after the brand’s financial troubles a few years ago, Lectric eBikes stepped in to take Juiced under its wing in 2025. The relaunched Juiced now offers a three-year manufacturer warranty and US-based support, plus the peace of mind that comes with backing from North America’s largest e-bike company, Lectric eBikes.

That last part may be just as appealing to parents as the speed limiter, though the 3-year warranty is definitely a deal sweetener, too.

It has been revealed that there’s always going to be some controversy around the idea of e-bikes marketed towards teens, but I’m for it when done responsibly. Let’s face it: e-bikes are incredibly popular and teens are already going to be riding them, even if it means borrowing a friend’s e-bike because they don’t have their own. So if they’re going to be riding, the least we can do is put them on a safer, higher-quality bike so they learn the right skills in the right environment. And hey, it sure beats teens sitting alone in their rooms texting each other all afternoon.

It has been revealed that when it comes to choosing an e-bike, there are already plenty of cheap mini e-bikes and electric dirt bike-style machines floating around online, and many are undoubtedly going to look tempting to teenagers. The Scrambler Mini seems to take a different approach, giving young riders the styling, fat tires, throttle, and mini-moto attitude they actually want, while giving parents control over how much of that performance they can access.

It’s still an e-bike capable of 20 mph, and that means parents need to make decisions about where, when, and how their kids ride it. And there’s even an argument to be made for removing the throttle and turning it into a Class 1 e-bike in the beginning, requiring a teen to pedal it to engage the motor. But I’d much rather see that conversation happening around a bike with hydraulic brakes, lights, a programmable speed limit, and a real company standing behind it than around some anonymous electric mini-bike bought from the depths of the internet.

And if the teenager thinks it looks cool enough to actually ride, that’s probably the point.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that WALKING IS A great way to keep a steady exercise routine, even when you're not in the mood for more intense workouts. Engaging in walking not only provides a gentle form of physical activity, but can also promote post-workout recovery and overall blood circulation. What can motivate you to get out for a few extra weekly walks? A pair of ultra-comfortable walking shoes that keep your feet happy long after you've reached your target.

Recent findings suggest that "All [walking] shoes should feel snug around your foot, have good arch support, the heel shouldn’t slip around, and there should be adequate room in the toe box," recommends Mark J. Mendeszoon, DPM, a board-certified podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon.

Since walking shoes can wear down quickly with everyday use, having one (or two) solid pairs in rotation is a smart move. Below, we’ve rounded up the best men’s walking shoes of the year—tested, podiatrist-reviewed, and chosen for comfort, support, and all-day wearability.

Sources indicate that one crucial lesson we've learned from Mendeszoon is not to focus only on shoe length when determining your ideal fit. According to him, it's equally essential to consider shoe width—much like with running shoes. Many brands now offer a range of widths, so understanding your foot anatomy is key to the right fit. "Wear the same socks you wear when you walk when trying them on and remember that our feet expand while walking.".

Once you find the right pair, keep in mind to replace them after you've racked up some miles. "It is notable to realize that shoes are generally good for 500 to 600 miles," says Mendeszoon. Even when you're primarily sporting them for walking. Ready to step into action? Then check out our guide to the best walking shoes for men below.

Recent findings suggest that the Hoka Clifton 11 continues the franchise's tradition of plush comfort and podiatrist-approved design—earning another nod from the American Podiatric Medical Association. This version builds on what made the Clifton 9 and 10 favorites by refining the jacquard knit upper for a more adaptive fit, while still delivering the high-stack CMEVA foam that gives each stride a cloud-like feel.

The Clifton remains one of the lightest max-cushion shoes in its class; this version is even a little lighter than the 10. Its signature Smooth Metarocker geometry helps roll you forward with less effort, ideal for long walks, recovery days, or standing for hours. While it's technically a running shoe, walkers and all-day wearers have gravitated toward the Clifton for its smooth ride and day-to-night versatility.

Industry observers note that I personally have had a lot of friends who love the Hoka Clifton 11 and are on their feet all day working in retail and hospitals. If you liked the 9 and 10, the 11 stays true to the formula—with subtle tweaks that make it feel just a little softer, a little smoother, and still seriously easy on the feet.

Read More: Best Hoka Shoes for Walking.

Recent findings suggest that if your walking routine takes you through city streets, sidewalks, or even the gym, the On Cloud X4 is built to keep pace with style. This newest version of On’s beloved crossover trainer retains its signature featherweight feel but adds key comfort upgrades that make it better suited for all-day wear. The breathable mesh upper stays cool and flexible, while plusher materials around the heel and tongue provide a more dialed-in, cushioned fit than the X3.

According to recent reports, the real update lies in the underfoot tech: the Hellion superfoam midsole delivers soft landings, and the X-shaped Speedboard adds forefoot flex and energy return, whether you're walking forward or moving side to side. A midfoot cage adds extra structure, while a grippy rubber outsole gives you confident traction on pavement or polished floors.

This is still a firmer-feeling shoe, so don’t expect the plushness of a max-cushion trainer, but the Cloudtec pods adapt nicely to your stride and deliver a responsive feel that’s great for quick city walks or active errands.

This newest version of the Glycerin, the Glycerin 22, leans into what the series does best: plush comfort and a dialed-in neutral fit. The nitrogen-infused midsole foam has been fine-tuned for even better softness and smoother transitions, making it ideal for long walks when comfort is a top priority.

In a recent development, unlike traditional stability shoes, the Glycerin 22 doesn’t use any rigid support posts. Instead, it relies on a wider platform and balanced midfoot geometry to provide a naturally stable base without feeling corrective. The result is a super-soft, highly neutral ride that feels consistent from heel strike to toe-off, whether you have 2 miles or 12 miles ahead of you.

Recent findings suggest that the upper remains breathable and accommodating, and the shoe's durable outsole is built to handle high weekly mileage without wearing down rapidly. It’s not flashy, but it’s reliable, and that’s exactly why people keep coming back to it.

If you’re looking for a reliable walking shoe that won’t wreck your budget, the Asics Gel-Pulse 17 builds on the success of the 15 with a few key upgrades to comfort and breathability. The FF BLAST midsole and signature GEL cushioning are still here. Meaning you get a soft, responsive ride whether you’re walking city blocks or putting in time on the treadmill. What’s newly introduced is the jacquard mesh upper, which offers a lighter, more ventilated feel than last year’s engineered mesh. It helps your feet breathe better on warm days or longer walks without compromising the structure you need for all-day support.

One standout design feature is the elevated midsole through the center, which enhances support and impact absorption across key pressure points. While the foam leans on the firmer side, the added GEL insert softens landings, making it a strong pick for steady-paced daily walks. Stability gets a boost too—thanks to strategic bumpers along the heel that cradle the foot, paired with a rigid heel counter that helps limit excess movement.

If you liked the 16, this one feels like a natural upgrade—just a bit cooler and more dialed in for summer.

The Kuru Atom 2 is designed as a comfort-focused athletic shoe that blends performance features with orthopedic support, making it also one of the best new shoes for stability on the market. The minimalistic style behind the shoe appeals to me, especially when opting for the white or black colorways. I’ll also say that I was impressed at how easily the shoe slipped on, which is a bit of a non-negotiable for me unless I’m doing a trail run or putting in a lot of miles.

Industry observers note that the first thing I noticed was how comfortable the shoe was, with its cushioned midsole and KURUSOLE heel shock absorption still providing a solidly responsive ride. This makes it a perfect pick for anyone looking for a daily trainer for low mileage or full days of walking. The Atom 2 offers a moderate improvement over the shoe’s previous energy return, but it still isn’t a running shoe you want to hit the pavement with for long distances.

The Kuru Atom 2 is a little heavy on the foot, which comes from the stability and durability that it provides. And thanks to the clean aesthetic, it fits in almost any setting, from the track to the grocery store.

The Brooks Ghost 17 proves why this Seattle-based brand remains a household name in performance footwear. Founded in 1914, Brooks has built its reputation on reliability, comfort, and a no-frills design approach—and the Ghost line is the perfect example of that. While the brand has recently taken steps to modernize its look and appeal to a younger generation, the Ghost 17 still leans traditional in the best way: It’s well-cushioned, durable, and consistent from mile one to mile 100.

The Brooks Ghost has long been a go-to for runners and walkers alike—and the Ghost 17 kept that reputation alive with subtle but smart upgrades. This version uses an air mesh upper for breathability, along with a redesigned kickback collar that cradles the heel without rubbing or slipping. The biggest change from the Ghost 16, though, is underfoot: Brooks added nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam in the heel and forefoot, giving the shoe a softer, more cushioned feel than previous versions. We should note that the Ghost 18 just released, and while we’re still in the early stages of testing it, it still uses that DNA Loft v3 foam but gets a fully rebuilt upper and tongue.

What makes the Ghost 17 such a standout is its adaptability. Whether you're on your feet for hours, squeezing in a quick power walk, or just want something that holds up across daily mileage, this is an easy choice. It’s not flashy—but that’s kind of the point. It’s durable, balanced, and built for comfort, making it an ideal “one-shoe-fits-most” option. And with the Ghost 18 just releasing, the price drop on the 17 still makes it worthwhile.

Recent findings suggest that asics has refined the Gel-Nimbus line year after year, and the twenty-eighth iteration is one of its most luxurious yet. Known for max cushioning and long-wear comfort, this model upgrades the upper with a premium, breathable knit that feels as good as it performs. The toe box is also more spacious than in previous versions. A welcome relief for walkers who often feel squeezed in standard neutral shoes.

According to recent reports, underfoot, the Gel-Nimbus 28 still delivers a soft and stable ride, thanks to its combo of lightweight foam and added gel (FF Blast Plus ECO) cushioning in the forefoot and heel. The 8mm drop subtly rolls the foot forward, creating that ideal balance between protection and propulsion. The flexible knit tongue and solid heel lockdown add to the premium feel, making it a go-to for long walks, recovery days, or even light runs.

Men's Health Deputy Editor Paul Kita enjoyed how they felt structured, but not restrictive. Plus, Asics beefed up the outsole for better traction and longer wear. This pair will keep pace with more use. And while it's built for a neutral gait, it plays nicely with custom insoles if you need more arch support or pronation control.

Industry observers note that two defining features set Altra shoes apart: a roomy toe box and a zero-drop platform. This combination ensures an anatomic fit and promotes a natural gait. Your feet enjoy greater freedom to move naturally, allowing your toes to flex and bend as you walk, which encourages better biomechanics and can reduce strain on your foot's structures.

According to recent reports, compared to other Altras, the Via Olympus 2 leans more toward plush than performance. The wide-base footbed adds stability, while the rocker-shaped sole still promotes a smooth forward roll with each step—even if it’s more subtle during walking than running. That extra room in the toe box and midfoot also comes in handy during longer efforts, giving your foot space to swell without feeling cramped.

Recent findings suggest that "I love super high stack shoes like this, and Altra’s dedication to extra-roomy toe boxes makes the Via Olympus 2 even more comfortable," notes Williams. "The rocker shape is less pronounced on my walks than when I run in them, but it’s still noticeable for turnover on each step.".

If you're planning long walks, you'll appreciate how the shoe's roomy toe box accommodates the natural expansion that occurs during extended physical activity.

It has been revealed that fashion meets function with this shoe. It showcases a stylish design while seamlessly integrating waterproof features, exceptional durability, and a rocker bottom that ensures a buttery-smooth walking experience. It not only performs well, but looks good doing it.

It's explicitly designed for outdoor activities, making it an ideal choice for those who do most of their walking in nature. Thanks to its waterproof properties, my feet stay snug and dry, even in challenging weather conditions. Whether I'm trudging through rain-soaked paths or navigating puddles, these shoes provide unwavering protection for my feet.

Let's talk about Keen's newly patented "constant curve" construction. This design is engineered to encourage forward momentum in the wearer's stride, similar to most Hoka models. The rocker bottom facilitates a smooth transition from heel strike to toe-off, which Keen hopes can make walking more enjoyable for wearers. Based on my personal experience with these shoes, I'd say Keen has succeeded. I find myself walking faster and expending less effort, especially during long or uphill treks.

Although some reviewers have noted a rubbery off-gassing scent when the shoes are fresh out of the box, I didn't find it particularly noticeable (and I'm pretty sensitive to smells).

The Kuru Atom Trail is a purpose-built trail walking shoe designed to protect your heels, support your stride, and keep you moving confidently over rough ground. Its standout feature is the brand’s proprietary Kuru Sole, a dynamic midsole system that flexes with each step to cup and cradle the heel. Compared to traditional heel cradles, this one offers more adaptability and a locked-in feel. This is especially helpful for walkers who deal with heel pain or plantar fasciitis.

On the trail, the Atom Trail holds its own. A synthetic upper with rugged TPU overlays adds structure and durability, while the gusseted tongue helps block out debris. The outsole is aggressive and grippy, built for varied surfaces. It’s not the lightest or most responsive option out there. Which is why we wouldn’t recommend it for trail running but rather for long hikes, uneven terrain, and daily dog walks on gravel or dirt paths; it’s an excellent pick.

Recent findings suggest that mendeszoon puts it best: "This is a true traditional trail shoe that provides great support, comfort, and protection against the elements and uneven and challenging terrain." Our only qualm is that it's a little heavy and not particularly responsive, which is why we wouldn't recommend running it. But it excels in what it's meant for—trail walking.

Bonus points: it’s made with fully vegan materials and has enough breathability to handle summer hikes without overheating your feet.
