💡 Key Takeaways
  • If there’s one thing I’ve learned as I’ve gotten older, it’s that being active and being strong aren’t necessarily the same thing.
  • I wanted everyday activities, like climbing stairs, carrying groceries, and getting up off the floor, to feel easier.
  • After a few weeks, I gradually incorporated 5- to 8-lb dumbbells into the movements, and a month or two later, I noticed a real difference in my strength: I could do more repetitions, lift even heavier weights, and move with greater confidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If there’s one thing I’ve learned as I’ve gotten older, it’s that being active and being strong aren’t necessarily the same thing. For most of my life, I’d been recreationally active, and had loved kayaking, swimming, and taking my dog on long walks. I’d never done any kind of structured strength training, until right before my 75th birthday. One day, I was sitting on a curb outside my house, and when it was time to stand up, I couldn’t. I felt embarrassed, and the idea of falling and not being able to get up or being in a situation where I couldn’t take care of myself was scary.

I wanted everyday activities, like climbing stairs, carrying groceries, and getting up off the floor, to feel easier. I also wanted to trust my body more, and feel confident in my ability to handle whatever life threw my way. So, I joined Aspire Athletic Club, a gym near my home in Schenectady, New York, and began working out once a week with the owner, Chris Wertman. In the beginning, even simple movements were challenging, so I started with basic bodyweight exercises like the box squat, step-up, and bird dog. The focus was on learning proper form and getting comfortable with the movements.

After a few weeks, I gradually incorporated 5- to 8-lb dumbbells into the movements, and a month or two later, I noticed a real difference in my strength: I could do more repetitions, lift even heavier weights, and move with greater confidence. It was so encouraging to see the hard work pay off, and it motivated me to keep going. About a year into consistent training, I was feeling stronger and ready to take on more. I began training full-body twice a week and incorporated more challenging exercises like squat variations, the walking lunge, weighted glute bridge, and chest fly to build overall strength.

I’d never deadlifted before, so seeing someone my age lift with that kind of strength was incredibly inspiring. That decision marked the beginning of a new chapter in my strength training journey—I told my new trainer of about six months, Jack Tyree, that I wanted to lift heavier weights and try deadlifting. I even began training for my gym’s upcoming annual deadlift exhibition, which was in eight months.

Since I’d just been training with dumbbells, I tried working with a kettlebell while I got comfortable with the movement and proper technique. As I got stronger and more confident, I graduated to the barbell and continued adding more weight each week. Then, this past May, I deadlifted 132 lbs for a single rep at the exhibition, setting a personal record. I never imagined I’d be able to do something like that, but I was so proud of how strong I’d become—and I was excited to see how much further I could push myself.

Sources indicate that six months after the exhibition, I now strength train three days a week: one day focused on upper body, one on lower body, and one dedicated to mobility and balance. Jack still programs all my workouts, and every session includes six to eight exercises, with 3 or 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps each. I use a mix of free weights and weight machines, and some of my go-to moves include the farmer’s carry, curtsy lunge, lat pulldown, scapular pushup, squat, and bench press. Deadlifts are still my favorite; I can now do three reps at 132 lbs, which I’m really proud of.

Outside the gym, I love getting outside and staying active, so I walk a few miles with my dog every day for my cardiovascular health. In addition to mobility and balance work at the gym, I also try to stretch at home whenever I can to ease muscle soreness and improve my range of motion, especially in my shoulders and hips.

It has been revealed that I know nutrition is an key part of recovery too. Although I don’t follow a strict nutrition plan or count macros, I try to eat protein at every meal to support muscle growth. Usually, it’s chicken, red meat, or a scoop of protein powder mixed into my morning oatmeal. I also prioritize whole foods and aim to incorporate a variety of fruits and vegetables throughout the day.

When I first started strength training, I didn’t know where to begin. So, having someone guide me through the movements, teach me proper form, and help me build strength safely made all the difference. My trainers have helped me recognize what I’m capable of, push beyond what I thought was possible, and progress at a pace that feels right. They also create workouts that challenge me while keeping my goals in mind. Having their support and encouragement has given me the confidence to try things I never imagined I could do. Whether it’s deadlifting heavy weights, bench pressing a barbell, or taking less rest between working sets, my trainers have taught me not to put a ceiling on what I think I can accomplish.

Recent findings suggest that before I strength trained, I felt weak and unsteady, but I didn’t give up and accept that I’d feel like that for the rest of my life. In some ways, I completely started over with exercise at 74 because I tried something brand newly introduced—and that’s affected my life outside of the gym.

Now, at 78, I feel stronger than ever; I can get up off the floor with ease, carry my own groceries into the house, shovel snow, garden, and play sports with my grandchildren. These are things I want to keep doing independently, and having the strength to do them confidently means the world to me. While I love lifting weights and hitting fresh PRs, the greatest reward is how much easier everyday life has become.

Learning to lift in my mid-70s wasn’t easy, and building that strength didn’t happen overnight, but I kept showing up, putting in the work, and gradually accomplishing what I once never thought was possible. Now, as I approach 80, I’m still getting stronger, and I want other women to know they’re never too old to get started, and they may be capable of far more than they realize. If I can go from struggling to get up from a curb to deadlifting 132 pounds, who knows what else is possible?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE HOLIDAYS AND GLP-1 can feel like a cruel joke. Mashed potatoes and gravy? Come on. Pumpkin pie? Dude. Your grandma’s urge to Eat! Eat! What’s wrong with you? It can be a lot.Luckily, we’re far enough along in this whole GLP-1 experience that researchers and experts now know how people who take the weight-loss medications can not only survive the holidays—but actually enjoy them, gravy and all. We talked to some of these smart people to come up with your GLP-1 game strategy—both at the table, and for around the table when those relatives you only see once a year get sassy.

Recent findings suggest that A POPULAR STRATEGY is to skip a dose for the holiday week. But doctors tend to recommend against this strategy.

Sources indicate that vijay Kasi, MD, PhD, cardiologist at Orlando Health says that you might even experience short-term changes in blood pressure and blood sugar spikes, which is really only a concern if you are diabetic. Now would missing one GLP-1 dose severely impact the heart? Not really.

Sources indicate that dr. Kasi states increased risk for cardiac events is more likely to happen when people quit the medication for good and slide back to unhealthy eating habits. A 2026 study found that any heart benefit from taking a GLP-1 disappears after two years. Those same people were linked to a 22 percent increased risk of stroke, heart attacks, and early death.

Recent findings suggest that but again, we’re talking about a week—not two years. So what’s wrong with resuming a day or two after the holiday? If you are still adamant about skipping a dose, resuming it immediately after is recommended. “If they ate a really large meal and then immediately took the medication, they may feel very uncomfortable,” notes Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center. “But if they wait 24 hours and the meal has moved through their system, then it probably won't be as problematic.”.

It has been revealed that the real concern doctors have is if people continue to delay their GLP-1 schedule for multiple weeks. Dr. Ali indicates people stop feeling the effects a week after they stop the medication because that’s how long it stays in your system. Appetite returns and so does food noise—the persistent and intrusive thoughts related to cravings or obsessing over how much food you ate. Ashley Koff, RD, author of Your Best Shot, says other problems that may promote overeating are that you no longer have a delay in gastric emptying and an alteration or sheer lack of fullness signaling. “When you stop this medication abruptly you go from [constant] sustained hormone back to your own which works at best for 2 to 5 minutes when triggered by food,” she says.

Sources indicate that while one day of eating more than usual won’t make a significant change to your health, Dr. Kasi indicates that some people do struggle to get back on track after the holidays end. “For a few people, it may be easy, but a vast majority trying to break away from their established regimen might have problems.”.

DOCTORS ARE GENERALLY against taking a smaller dose than usual because it is not included in FDA guidelines for how to safely and effectively use a GLP-1. “If a lower dose wasn't effective for you beforehand, it's not going to be effective for you right before a holiday either,” indicates Dr. Ali. “It’s similar to skipping a dose.”.

There is one exception. Dr. Ali claims people who have attained a healthy weight or reached their goal weight may be able to lower their dose or take it less frequently as a maintenance strategy.

According to recent reports, “For some people who have been on it for a long time, they titrate down to the most effective dose,” says Heidi Skolnik, MS, CDN, nutritionist and author of Your GLP-1 Game Blueprint. “You're trying to find what's the lowest amount that still is effective for you.”.

Sources indicate that lowering your GLP-1 dose is a conversation you’ll want to have with your doctor ahead of the holiday season. Experts say to avoid self-prescribing.

IF YOU’RE ON a GLP-1, your plate will likely look different from your relatives who are scooping up major portions of carb-heavy sides. With a lower tolerance for small portions and a change in appetite, your choices will involve a delicate balance of trying to meet your nutritional needs while also not making your stomach hurt from overindulging. You can, of course, still enjoy as many courses as you like.

Industry observers note that if you are going to someone’s house, Skolnik advises calling ahead and asking what’s on the menu so you can strategy in advance. For appetizers, you’ll want to avoid any high-fat items. “It's okay if you don't hit your protein and fiber goals. But what you don't want to do is eat a lot of high fat,” she says. “This is because your gastric system is slowing down. With high-fat foods, you may not digest all of that.”.

Not sure what’s high-fat or not? Play it safe and bring your own appetizer. Not only are you being a hospitable guest, but you’ll have something you can eat. Skolnik recommends:.

Don’t think that you’re banned from eating any certain foods, but with small portions, you have to know if it’s worth indulging. Koff notes to use the "Delicious to Me" rule. Stop after the first bite to assess how much you enjoy the food. “I give them what that means on a scale they devise from 1 to 10, where a 7 or greater means it’s delicious and a go.”.

Sources indicate that so include those carb-heavy sides like mac and cheese and creamy mashed potatoes—just keep it to around a quarter of your plate. The majority of your plate should include a mix of vegetables and protein, which Skolnik states is usually manageable with turkey.

Common side effects of GLP-1 use include nausea from drinking and a reduced craving for alcohol. If you can tolerate one or two, both dietitians say to go for it. A drinking variation of the “Delicious to Me” strategy is the “9 Sips” rule. “You still need to factor in what sugar, caffeine, and alcohol will do but a smaller amount is the win while still enjoying,” says Koff. You’ll also want to drink water at regular intervals while you’re drinking.

If you want to avoid being pressured into drinking, Skolnik claims to also have a drink on hand with a lime slice to give the appearance of an alcoholic drink. “Nobody has to know what's in your glass.”.

Recent findings suggest that no need to ruin a favorite dessert by trying to choose only high-protein items. If you want to save your appetite for an extra slice of pie, Koff says to go for it. Just make sure to meet your nutritional needs in different ways as with a protein drink before dinner or supplements.

IT’S NOT JUST the food you need to navigate; the interactions matter too. Depending on your family situation, you may need to set some firm boundaries on or redirect comments related to your weight or appetite. That doesn’t mean the holidays are the time to announce to everyone you’re on a GLP-1 (unless you want to). Some phrases you can use include:.

Skolnik says having an ally is extremely key if you’re expecting other people to comment on your eating habits or your looks. They can help to redirect any uncomfortable conversation, provide support for your choices so you don’t feel isolated, or just provide emotional support. “Have someone else in the room with a code word or a look that signals them to intervene and change the conversation or divert attention away,” she says.

According to recent reports, even if you don’t have an ally physically next to you, have someone available on the phone that you can text or call. Skolnik says to escape to the bathroom if you need and use it as a place to recenter.

To avoid offending people who probably spent hours cooking, it can also be helpful to practice polite ways to turn down second helpings or pass on specific dishes.

“When the giving of food is looked at as love, the receiving of it is love,” says Skolnik. “But you can still receive the love without the food.”.

Rejecting Oppression, Embracing Joy

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • What makes a literary character—or a living person you’ve just met—seem intensely human?
  • In a recent study of over 400 readers, 19 percent reported “experiential crossing” in which the language and characters of a book they were reading entered their daily lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

What makes a literary character—or a living person you’ve just met—seem intensely human? Besides the movements people make and the sensations they describe, their attitudes can show their humanity. In literature, characters who resist social oppression make more compelling protagonists than those who quietly occupy a society's bottom rungs. Most inspiring of all may be characters shocked by abuse because, despite poverty, sexism, and racism, they believe they deserve joyful lives.

In a recent study of over 400 readers, 19 percent reported “experiential crossing” in which the language and characters of a book they were reading entered their daily lives. “It’s as if the character has started to narrate my world,” wrote one participant (Alderson-Day et al. 2017). Getting to know literary characters can broaden readers’ understandings of human life if those characters’ experiences differ from readers' own.

Sources indicate that when characters’ experiences match those of readers, their crossover into readers’ worlds can feel life-affirming, especially if their experiences rarely appear in published fiction. At a book signing in Cambridge, a woman thanked author Junot Díaz for creating Beli, a central character in his novel The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao. “I had a life a lot like Beli’s,” the reader told him. Tears kept her from saying more (Díaz 2018).

According to recent reports, born in the Dominican Republic, Belicia (Beli) Cabral is sold as a child after her mother dies and her father is imprisoned for offending the dictator, Rafael Trujillo. During her nine years as a slave, her “father” burns her back with hot oil when she tries to attend school. After a distant relative rescues Beli, she grows into a tall, strikingly beautiful young woman. A relationship with Trujillo’s brother-in-law wrecks her life, however, when his henchmen force her to have an abortion and beat her nearly to death. She escapes to Newly introduced Jersey, where she marries, but her husband abandons her and their two children. To support her son and daughter, she works several minimum-wage jobs, persisting even after she develops breast cancer. Beli is abusive and violent not just to her children but to neighbors, shoppers, and police officers. Throughout her life, she retains her sense of self-worth, refusing to believe she should be exploited because she is female, Dominican, and Black.

According to recent reports, recent studies affirm that the suppressed emotions caused by social inequality harm people’s physical and mental health (Kiehl 2024). The effects of racism have received more attention than those of social class, whose influence many people still deny (Kiehl 2024). Beli and readers who see their lives in hers experience disrespect caused by sexism as well. Her ability to inspire readers stems not from her suffering, however, but from her sense that she is inferior to no one and deserves a good life.

Industry observers note that junot Díaz’s character-narrator, Yunior, hints that Beli can’t see disaster coming because even after being enslaved and burned, she can’t imagine how badly people will treat her. “Like everybody in this damn story,” he writes, “she underestimated the depth of the shit she was in” (Díaz 2007). Beli’s refusal to accept that she is in danger shows not just her sense of self-worth but her belief (at least in her youth) in other people’s goodness. Yunior illustrates her capacity for joy, which blazes forth in her dancing. A complex character, Beli terrorizes her neighborhood and hurts her children, but her humanity is never in doubt. Her will to survive and her rejection of abuse ensure that whether or not readers see themselves in her, she will enter and inhabit their lives.

According to recent reports, like lay readers, psychologists can learn from imagining Beli because in creating characters, authors build models of minds (Alderson-Day et al. 2017; Bernini 2021). Participants in psychological experiments still come disproportionately from “WEIRD” (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) populations, especially North American and European universities (Henrich et al. 2010). Novels like Díaz’s Oscar Wao guide readers to imagine the mental world of a woman who experiences horrors but retains her self-worth and desire for joy. Until scientific studies can include more of the world’s population, literature can complement information revealed through experiments by making a wider range of human experiences imaginable. Most human of all may be the belief that no matter how other people see you, you deserve to thrive.

Iceland’s first wind farm comes with a water-saving bonus

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.
  • Vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads.
  • Landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power firm, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.

Vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads. And Iceland’s windiest months coincide with the time of year when less water flows into its reservoirs.

Landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power firm, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026. The first 14 turbines are online; another 14 will be installed in a second phase, and the entire wind farm is expected to be operating by the end of 2027.

Once complete, Vaðölduver will have 120 megawatts (MW) of capacity. When I met with the folks at Landsvirkjun in Reykjavik last month, they told me that’s enough to power the equivalent of 90,000 Icelandic households. Vaðalda’s electricity feeds into the grid and is sold through power purchase agreements.

Vaðölduver sits on a lava-and-sand plain east of the Þjórsá River, south of Sultartangi Dam. Landsvirkjun already operates seven hydropower stations in the surrounding Þjórsá and Tungnaá region.

The wind farm was sited in this region of Iceland because the seasons line up nicely.

The winds are strongest in winter, when inflows into hydropower reservoirs can be low. In summer, wind speeds tend to drop, but glacial melt increases water availability for the hydropower system.

Industry observers note that when the wind turbines are generating plenty of electricity, Landsvirkjun can ease off hydropower and leave more water in its reservoirs. When the wind drops, hydropower can pick up more of the demand.

That gives the utility more control over when it uses its stored water and helps that water go further.

In a recent development, german wind turbine maker Enercon manufactured Vaðölduver’s turbines. The project also includes a service and maintenance agreement with Enercon.

According to recent reports, landsvirkjun had a decade of experience operating pilot wind turbines before building Vaðölduver. One big thing they learned: They didn’t need tall towers to find plenty of wind.

Sources indicate that there’s little vegetation or other surface obstructions across this unique, exposed landscape. That allows the turbines to capture productive winds closer to the ground than they could at a more wooded or sheltered location.

“Lower” is relative, of course. The turbines still reach 150 meters (492 feet) at their highest blade tip.

The wind farm covers 17.1 square kilometers (6.6 square miles). Twenty-five turbines are rated at 4.26 MW each, and the remaining three at 4.5 MW. Landsvirkjun’s presentation puts annual generation at 440 GWh and lists a P50 net efficiency figure of 43%, which is considered strong for onshore wind.

The ability to tap into existing infrastructure was a major factor in Landsvirkjun’s site selection. Where a wind farm goes affects its cost, its environmental footprint, and the people who live nearby.

Landsvirkjun also identifies active engagement with communities and other stakeholders as essential to building wind projects. At Vaðölduver, the immediate task is to finish the remaining 14 turbines while the first phase completes its trial runs.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer sees wind as a potential third pillar of Iceland’s electricity supply alongside hydropower and geothermal. Vaðölduver reveals how those resources can work together, with wind adding generation while helping conserve stored water.

According to recent reports, iceland is a world leader in clean energy. It generates nearly 100% of its electricity from renewable sources, combining hydropower fueled by glacial runoff and rivers (around 70%) and geothermal energy (around 30%).

Over 90% of Icelandic households use direct geothermal hot water for space heating and hot water, while the remaining homes use renewable electricity.

But it’s got the same grid capacity challenges as every other country. Adding wind – and anything else that uses power – means paying close attention to what the grid can handle. Iceland has an isolated transmission system, so maintaining stability and ensuring sufficient capacity are increasingly crucial as the country develops more projects.

In a recent development, while in Reykjavik, I met with the Minister of the Environment, Energy and Climate, Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson, who told me that the Icelandic grid’s capacity is expected to grow from 20 TWh to 24-25 TWh within a decade. Jóhannsson also said that he is pro-data center and that investors are keen to establish more of them in the country.

When I asked Jóhannsson and his team, as well as the teams at Landsvirkjun and publicly owned ON Power, Iceland’s second-largest electricity generator and largest EV charger network, about grid expansion plans to handle that pipeline, they all noted that legislative reforms were being passed to speed up energy permitting processes. There is also financing in place to grow the grid. The physical transmission network is being expanded, but the process is slow because NIMBYism is creating bottlenecks.

In learning about newly introduced and completed Icelandic power projects during my visit, it was apparent that the companies in the power and geothermal heat sector regularly collaborate on projects – everyone brings their expertise to the table and works for the common good (yes, really).

But what was striking in discussions about grid expansion was that there seemed to be no plans to pitch in with the Icelandic transmission system operator (TSO), Landsnet hf. It seemed that the plan was to let the TSO come up with the solutions on its own. At most, Jóhannsson’s team stated its legislative reform “opened the door” to possible grid innovations.

When I asked the Landsvirkjun team whether they were considering working with the TSO on distributed energy resource (DER) projects like virtual power plants and onsite battery storage for its heavy-industry clients, which make up 80% of its business, they said they hadn’t considered it.

Recent findings suggest that I often wonder why Quebec hasn't followed this strategy. They have huge dams with world-leading power connections, and one of the issue they are facing is a lack of water to refill those dams, due to several years of relative drought. I know it costs a lot to build wind power up north, but siting a project there would re-use their massive investment in power lines. The dams would act as gigantic batteries, because they wouldn't need to drain their reservoirs when the wind is blowing.

Recent findings suggest that iceland has earned its reputation as a clean energy leader. Bringing that same collaborative and creative approach to expanding its grid would help it keep setting an example for the rest of the world.

Even Alaska’s bears are not immune from accidentally making things weird or getting a bit too close. Over the summer, rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska watched an odd interaction between two unnamed black bears (Ursus americanus) taking part in Anan Creek’s salmon run.

According to recent reports, “Sometimes the bears at Anan share the creek… a little too closely,” the rangers write. “One bear is waiting his turn for a prime fishing spot, and the other is so focused on the fish he doesn’t mind his surroundings. Did the 1st bear make it weird by backing up, or did the 2nd bear make it weird by staying there?”.

For this bit of humor, the rangers awarded the unnamed bears with the 2026 You Made it Weird Award.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Recent findings suggest that the largest national forest in the United States, Tongass covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in the region. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

According to recent reports, the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

According to recent reports, police in Canada say they have busted an organized auto theft crime ring that was stealing cars from the Great White North and shipping them across the ocean to Africa. Authorities announced a total of over 200 charges against 12 arrested individuals associated with the crime. In addition, officers recovered more than 90 vehicles worth a combined $4.5 million Canadian—$3.15 million in U.S. dollars.

In a recent development, while the charges and announcement came on Monday, authorities have been putting this case together since March, when officers of the Peel Regional Police in Ontario put together what they called “Project Cadetta” in partnership with the Canada Border Services Agency. Together, they initially focused on a single warehouse in Brampton, which allegedly was the staging area for stolen cars that were destined for West Africa via Canadian shipping ports. As police investigated the space, they began linking individuals to other locations.

Authorities say that many of these cars would get different VIN numbers as a part of the scheme. While they didn't detail the vehicles in question, they did show photos of a few; among them are several Lexus vehicles, a Land Rover Range Rover Sport, a Toyota Land Cruiser, and a BMW XM.

If this sounds familar, it’s not just you; this year alone, we at Road & Track have reported on similar theft rings several times. In April, authorities in the U.S. charged six people with being part of an illegal operation to steal cars and ship them to Africa. Police linked the suspects to some 130 cars. Then, later in the same month, police in New York stated they found 72 more cars destined for West Africa. The cars in question included a Rolls-Royce, several BMWs, and an Audi SQ8. In May, Canadian police found another 40 stolen cars involved with a similar theft ring.

It has been revealed that THE ENDORPHINS, the physical changes you can see and feel in your body, the overall confidence boost that comes with doing something good for your body—yeah, the benefits of working out are hard to beat. The one area where a sweat session can fall short, however, is when it comes to the health of our nails.

According to recent reports, if you're someone who loves a fresh manicure, especially one with some length, you know the struggle of keeping your tips intact at the gym. Between chipped polish, cracks and peeling, and the mental gymnastics of trying to avoid both, it can sometimes feel like your nails (and your sanity) are getting a workout of their own. “When I’m lifting plates or handling weights, I’m always conscious of how I’m gripping,” shares celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador Gina Edwards, who's a frequent gym-goer herself. “I use my finger pads rather than the tips of my fingers to help avoid putting unnecessary pressure on my nails.”.

Recent findings suggest that meet the experts: Gina Edwards is a celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador. Dana Stern, MD, is a Upcoming York-based dermatologist who specializes in nail disorders. Marisa Garshick, MD, is a dermatologist based in New York City. Jin Soon Choi is a celebrity manicurist in New York City.

Industry observers note that not into manicures? Unfortunately, that doesn't mean you're completely off the hook. Even bare nails can take a beating: “The nail is a thousand times more absorptive of water than the skin,” indicates Upcoming York dermatologist Dana Stern, MD, who specializes in nail disorders. And because frequent handwashing and exposure to moisture often go hand in hand with working out, nails are subjected to expansion as they absorb water and contraction as they dry. “Repeated wet-dry cycles can contribute to splitting and peeling, particularly in people already prone to brittle nails,” Dr Stern adds.

But not to worry—you don’t have to choose between having polished digits and getting your fitness on. With a few smart habits, you can avoid all the pitfalls. Here’s how.

It has been revealed that no matter how you choose to work out, there are plenty of ways your nails can suffer. And most of us don't even realize we're putting them in harm's way until it's too late. Maybe you're in a workout class, engaging in some friendly competition with your neighbor to see who can knock out their burpees the fastest, only to jam a nail as your hands hit the ground. Or perhaps the damage happens before you even break a sweat. Picture it: You're pulling on your most compressive pair of leggings when a nail snags on the fabric or, worse, bends backward and breaks.

Sources indicate that of course, some activities pose a more obvious risk than others. Exercises that involve “repetitive gripping, pressure, or friction, such as weightlifting, rock climbing, and certain types of strength training” can be especially hard on your nails, says Marisa Garshick, MD, a dermatologist based in Newly introduced York City.

Here are a few of the ways your workout routine might be doing a number on them:.

Handling dumbbells, weight plates, and other equipment can put pressure on nails, especially if they're long, dry, or already weak, indicates celebrity manicurist Jin Soon Choi.

Recent findings suggest that jamming a nail against a hard surface or repeatedly putting pressure on it can cause the nail plate to separate from the nail bed, a condition known as onycholysis. This can happen to natural nails, too, although extensions may create additional opportunities for snagging.

When a falsie gets caught on something, it can even cause the underlying natural nail to lift from the nail bed, explains Dr. Stern. Depending on the extent of the damage, it can take months for a healthy latest nail to grow in.

Recent findings suggest that frequent handwashing and exposure to harsh cleansers (including those used to wipe down gym equipment and alcohol-based hand sanitizers) can contribute to splitting and peeling, Dr. Stern adds.

It has been revealed that while running and cycling may be gentler on your hands, repeated pressure inside athletic shoes can cause bruising beneath the nail (known as a subungual hematoma), thickening, or even nail loss, explains Dr. Garshick.

The good news? Most workout-related nail damage is temporary, provided the nail matrix, which is responsible for nail growth, hasn't been damaged. But more serious injuries can have lasting consequences. A crush injury—heavy weight falling on a nail, for example—could cause permanent damage to the nail matrix, Dr. Stern notes. Even when the damage isn't permanent, patience is key. According to Dr. Garshick, fingernails typically take three to six months to grow out, while toenails can take twelve to eighteen months.

Recent findings suggest that the goal isn't to give up your favorite workouts or your favorite manicures. A few tweaks to your nail-care routine and how you handle equipment can make all the difference.

Here's what the pros recommend to keep your nails looking and feeling their best.

This ultra-nourishing product delivers a healthy dose of barrier-repairing ceramides, hyaluronic acid, and niacinamide sans greasy residue.

Jinsoon Primrose + Honeysuckle Healing Cuticle Oil.

Choi recommends this product, from her own line, before bed to help maintain healthy nails and cuticles.

OPI Repair Mode Bond Building Nail Serum.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve heard of bond builders for hair, right? This is the same thing, but for nails. It promises longer, stronger nails in just four weeks.

It’s vital to keep in mind that Dr. Garshick says not every nail change is workout-related. Persistent discoloration, thickening, or lifting can sometimes indicate a fungal infection, psoriasis, or another nail condition. A latest or changing dark streak, particularly one that doesn't grow out, should also be evaluated by a board-certified dermatologist.

Sources indicate that at the end of the day, you don't have to choose between crushing your fitness goals and keeping your nails in good shape. In fact, Choi points out that exercise itself can actually be beneficial for nail health, as physical activity promotes healthy circulation, helping deliver oxygen and nutrients to the tissues responsible for nail growth.

It's the accidental injuries and repeated pressure that can cause problems, not the workouts themselves. With a few simple adjustments to your nail-care routine and a bit more awareness of how you're handling equipment, you can keep breaking a sweat without breaking a nail.

The Naked Truth About Taking Your Inner Ape for a Walk

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • It has been revealed that walking is a key milestone for human development, an activity done for recreation, and can be an Olympic sport.
  • It has been revealed that A key characteristic of human gait is that we land on our heels at the end of swing—something found also in African apes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

It has been revealed that walking is a key milestone for human development, an activity done for recreation, and can be an Olympic sport. Walking is a critical and integral behavior across the animal kingdom. It's also something that can be leveraged with deliberate practice. And it's been going on for millions of years since our proto-human ancestors were learning to stand upright, walk bipedally, and land on their heels.

It has been revealed that A key characteristic of human gait is that we land on our heels at the end of swing—something found also in African apes. My research career included diving deep into the neuromechanics of human walking and especially the way sensory feedback and spinal cord motor control vary functionally while we move. I was fascinated by the fact that the most critically controlled part of the step cycle is heel strike—just when your foot lands and weight begins to shift onto the new stance leg.

In a recent development, so my eye was drawn to the recent work, "Heel-strike Mechanics Reveal Evolutionary Trade-offs in Hominin Bipedalism" by Nicholas B. Holowka et al.

It has been revealed that these researchers studied bipedal and quadrupedal locomotion of chimpanzees and humans and examined forces and angles of the foot at the beginning of stance. They found that chimpanzees had much larger ranges of foot-strike angles than humans and often did not land heel-first.

Impact forces and loading rates are much higher with heel-striking, but metabolic cost is lower. This work suggests that the primitive leg anatomy of early hominins meant either high impact forces or poor walking economy. A convergent solution for less mechanically stressful, more economical, and larger travel ranges arrived via "evolution of larger heels and lower limb joints.".

But can we turn heel-strike walking into striking with our heels? The timing of when you put your foot down at heel strike is the most dangerous part of the entire step cycle. If we make a mistake, or we slip on something, or the ground gives when we put our heel down and our body begins to shift weight onto that leg, we can have a catastrophic failure and a fall. Which is the ultimate failure for the locomotive system.

According to recent reports, so it's critical to avoid a catastrophe, and evolution of bipedal locomotion has incorporated neurological connections that assist in controlling this. But the opposite side of that is that it's also an opportunity. And that's where self-protection and martial arts training factor in.

In a recent development, that critical part of the step cycle is an excellent time to take that heel and stomp it onto an attacker's instep or the top of their foot. You can jam all your weight that's already moving forward to normally be accepted by your stance leg. But now it's to destabilize your opponent.

Sources indicate that this is something I teach when guiding martial arts practice: harnessing the natural movement of the body as the base layer for tactical reaction. Martial arts like Bagua Zhang center core practice on circle walking, where locomotion is central to the performance of discrete actions. We can connect our evolutionary advantage in walking to become a powerful application of self-protective action. This allows us to fully express the functional connectivity within the nervous system, mostly subliminal and automatic, in deliberate mindful action.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that be wary of the next few shortened website links you click on social media.
  • That’s a polite way of putting it, since many of the hijacked URLs sent unsuspecting people on detours to inappropriate, obscene, and offensive webpages ranging from Wikipedia entries on the Holocaust and 9/11, to vulgar YouTube audio clips.
  • It has been revealed that link-shortening is one of the internet’s simplest and most convenient workarounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that be wary of the next few shortened website links you click on social media. According to the service provider Bitly, its hyperlinks in older tweets from many companies, politicians, and even government accounts are now redirecting to “content unrelated to the original posts.”.

That’s a polite way of putting it, since many of the hijacked URLs sent unsuspecting people on detours to inappropriate, obscene, and offensive webpages ranging from Wikipedia entries on the Holocaust and 9/11, to vulgar YouTube audio clips.

It has been revealed that link-shortening is one of the internet’s simplest and most convenient workarounds. The service typically works by pinning a website’s lengthy, complex URL address to a tidied-up, abbreviated shortcut in a digital registry. This shortened address then redirects anyone who clicks it to their intended online destination.

It has been revealed that well…in theory. Security analysts have tried to warn people about an issue known as “bit rot” for decades. In 2009—about one year after Bitly’s debut—Silicon Valley entrepreneur Joshua Schacter wrote a prescient blog post cautioning against what he felt were potentially serious flaws in the link-shortening “middleman” system. Amid the problems, Schacter cited a “new and potentially unreliable” tool that ties an original hyperlink to the “health of a third party.”.

It has been revealed that “The shortener may decide a link is a Terms Of Service violation and delete it. If the shortener accidentally erases a database, forgets to renew its domain, or just disappears, the link will break,” he explained. “If a top-level domain changes its policy on commercial use, the link will break. If the shortener gets hacked, every link becomes a potential phishing attack.”.

It now appears bad actors recently identified countless of these Bitly links previously posted across social media between 2009 and 2014. Although their exact methods aren’t clear, it’s possible they generated their own custom Bitly links using the addresses in the social media posts, then used those to send people to different destinations. Bitly claims its links do not automatically expire, but paid users may redirect existing links.

Industry observers note that many examples were found among the more than 60,000 posts on X from President Donald Trump’s official account. In one of Trump’s previous posts about his golf course in Scotland, the Bitly link temporarily redirected to Wikipedia’s entry on the Epstein Files. Targets also included corporations like McDonald’s, with one of the fast food giant’s 2011 Bitly URLs suddenly linked to Wikipedia’s page about the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

Not every hijacked post funneled people to upsetting outcomes. Instead of a cybersecurity PSA, the Bitly address in a 2021 post from the FBI briefly linked to a photo of a blubbery seal. Another of Trump’s URLs sent you to the popular video game, Geometry Dash.

In its acknowledgement of the problem on November 15, Bitly reported it had identified and suspended the bad actors’ accounts, and were in the process of “disabling the affected links.”.

“Our Trust and Safety team is working to address the issue and strengthen protections against similar misuse in the future,” Bitly wrote at the time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that old solar panels have silver and copper worth recovering. A new US recycling company called Jupiter prepares to send metals recovered from retired solar panels and data center hardware to Korea Zinc’s refineries, including a $7.4 billion plant planned for Clarksville, Tennessee.

Jupiter joins US solar panel recycler Solarcycle and PedalPoint Recycling, Korea Zinc’s US recycling and metals business, into a single, fully integrated organization. Jupiter notes it’s launching with eight certified US facilities, nearly 1 million square feet of processing space, and about 250 employees. It’s also taking on customers from both businesses, including Microsoft, Prologis, and Brookfield.

Industry observers note that for a solar farm or data center operator, that means a single tech giant can take equipment out of service, resell parts with remaining useful life, and recycle the rest. Customers can track where the materials go and bring them back into their own supply chains.

Korea Zinc will hold a majority stake. Solarcycle’s Suvi Sharma will lead Jupiter as CEO, and PedalPoint’s Kevin Hahm will be CFO. Microsoft and Prologis Ventures are among Solarcycle’s existing investors.

As Electrek reported in January, Solarcycle’s Cedartown, Georgia, plant was processing thousands of old solar panels a week when it opened. Solarcycle said the plant could handle up to 5 gigawatts’ worth of panels annually at full capacity, recovering materials such as glass, aluminum, copper, and silver.

The Tennessee plant adds a US refining step. Korea Zinc is developing the facility, called Project Crucible, with US government backing. It expects to start production in phases in 2029. The plant is designed to process about 1.1 million tons of raw materials per year and produce roughly 540,000 tons of finished products.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, upcoming research suggests.

In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.

They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million latest cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.

In the United States, this simple salt swap could prevent nearly 105,000 deaths and about 492,000 upcoming cases a year, the researchers estimated.

About 130.6 million U.S. adults have cardiovascular disease, according to the American Heart Association (AHA).

Liping Huang, PhD, a senior data analyst in the Food Policy Division at The George Institute for Global Health and co-lead author of the study, told Healthline the team started with current blood pressure levels by sex, age, and country.

The researchers then estimated how replacing all salt with a salt substitute would change people’s sodium and potassium intake, blood pressure, and disease risk, she said.The team modeled a blend of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride. The study estimated these yearly results worldwide:.

The authors wrote that the model relied on data from a few years ago and on many assumptions, and that any large-scale switch would take years.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride, according to The George Institute.Asked where other salts like kosher salt and sea salt fit in, Huang mentioned those salts may contain some trace elements “which has those health halos around them, but essentially they’re still primarily sodium chloride.”Huang noted that potassium-enriched salt tastes “about the same as a regular table salt.” She said it’s possible a small number of people with a sensitive palate could taste a difference.

It has been revealed that huang stated that “it’s really hard for people to cut back their salt intake.”“But the easier way is just to replace part of the sodium chloride in our normal salt with potassium chloride, because increasing potassium intake also helps to reduce blood pressure,” she said.The two minerals play opposite roles in the body, according to Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“While sodium causes water retention and increased blood pressure, potassium will help the kidneys remove sodium from the body and lower blood pressure,” Chen told Healthline.Huang stated she worked on an earlier trial of about 21,000 people in 600 rural villages in northern China in 2021.

People who used potassium-enriched salt had a 14% lower risk of stroke, a 13% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 12% lower risk of early death than those who used regular salt, according to a 2021 study in The Latest England Journal of Medicine that summarized the trial’s results.

The World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt in a 2025 guideline, saying it can reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Industry observers note that the AHA said potassium-based salt substitutes can help lower blood pressure in some adults. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued labeling guidance in 2020 allowing an alternate name for potassium chloride on ingredient labels to include the word “salt.”“We think that blood pressure begins to improve as soon as 1 week after cutting back on sodium intake. The full benefit typically takes up to 4 weeks,” Chen said.

It has been revealed that “We generally recommend a daily sodium limit of 2,300 milligrams (mg), ideally under 1,500 mg a day. Most people consume over 3,000 mg of sodium a day, well above the recommended limit,” Chen said.The WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day and suggests at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day.In the United States, more than 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, according to the AHA.

Huang stated that some people with advanced chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium-enriched salt.When the kidneys don’t work well, the body may not clear extra potassium efficiently, she said. That can lead to hyperkalemia, or high potassium levels in the blood, which can raise the risk of cardiac arrest, Huang said.Among people with stage 3 to stage 5 kidney disease, switching to salt substitutes could prevent about 750,000 deaths a year by lowering blood pressure and cause about 100,000 deaths a year from hyperkalemia, the researchers estimated.The AHA said that people with kidney disease or who take medications that affect potassium should check with a healthcare professional before using these products.

An estimated 37 million U.S. adults have chronic kidney disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Sources indicate that potassium-enriched salt is available at supermarkets in the U.S. Many major U.S. grocery chains, including Kroger, Walmart, and Publix, carry two types of products, according to their websites:.

Potassium-enriched salt typically costs about twice as much as regular salt, according to the study.Huang mentioned she hoped people would see the results and start thinking of the switch as “a simple thing I can do for their own health.”.

Henry Ford was racing cars before the Mustang, GT40, or even the Ford Motor Manufacturer itself existed. Back in 1901, he won his first race behind the wheel of a two-cylinder race car nicknamed “Sweepstakes,” a car that produced just 26 horsepower. 125 years later, Ford has unveiled the 815-horsepower 2028 Mustang GTD 1901—a special edition inspired by the car that helped launch Henry Ford's automotive empire.

Sources indicate that the Mustang GTD 1901 has a 789-horsepower advantage over the Sweepstakes car, but the design inspiration is clear. The Mustang GTD 1901 features a distinctive Royal Red exterior and a wide, off-center black racing stripe featuring a bright red centerline. The color combination reverses the original race car's black body and deep red chassis components. Additional diagonal graphics and exposed carbon-fiber elements, including the front splitter, rocker panels, rear diffuser, and wing, complete the exterior look.

It has been revealed that have a seat inside the Mustang GTD 1901, and you immediately realize this is not an ordinary GTD—that is, if there is even such a thing as an ordinary GTD. The first thing you notice are the Mahogany Red leather seats with Race Red stitching. Keep looking, and you’ll see there are also matching red accents on the seatbelts, while the steering wheel receives Mahogany Red faux suede.

The Performance Package is standard equipment on the Mustang GTD 1901. Options include the magnesium wheels, which reduce the unsprung weight by 50.3 pounds. If you want to spice up the interior, you can order the optional titanium trim package, which gets you redesigned titanium shifter paddles that have been lengthened for the 2028 model year. The titanium trim in the GTD, by the way? It comes from retired F-22 fighter jets.

Ford has not announced how many Mustang GTD 1901’s will be built, or how much they will cost. But we wouldn’t count on seeing too many at your local track day.

In a recent development, A lot has changed since Henry Ford won his first race; horsepower figures, aerodynamics, and suspension technology have come a long way. But the desire of the company that bears his name to prove itself on the racetrack apparently hasn't changed much at all, and that’s something we’re certainly thankful for.

#109767. How To Build Strength You’ll Actually Use In Daily Life, According To A Trainer

How To Build Strength You’ll Actually Use In Daily Life, According To A Trainer

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym.
  • As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.
  • Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym. It helps make everyday tasks easier, whether that's carrying heavy shopping bags and moving furniture or putting a suitcase in the overhead compartment on a flight.

As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.

Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.

By focusing on simple, functional movements that mimic everyday activities, you can build strength that carries over into daily life and keeps you strong, active and confident as you get older.

“It's not necessary to spend hours lifting weights to build strength that makes a difference,” he explains. “Even two or three strength sessions a week can help, especially when you're focusing on compound exercises that work several muscle groups at once.”.

Squats are one of the best exercises for building lower-body strength because—as a compound exercise—they work your thighs, glutes, and core all at once.

“These are the muscles you use when getting up from a chair, lifting something off the floor or crouching down to do some gardening,” says Carr. Keeping them strong can make a real difference to how easily you move around, particularly as you get older.

Step-ups are great for building leg strength and improving balance at the same time, says Carr.

Industry observers note that “They're particularly useful for everyday activities like climbing stairs, walking uphill, or stepping onto curbs. As we age, maintaining strength and stability in our legs becomes increasingly important, and step-ups are a simple way to work on both,” he adds.

Farmer's carries are a brilliant exercise for building strength you actually use, because they're essentially the same movement as carrying heavy shopping bags.

“They work your grip, shoulders and core, helping you carry things more comfortably and with better stability. Grip strength can decline with age, so it's a really useful exercise to include in your routine,” states Carr.

Picking something up, whether it's a laundry basket, a suitcase or a bag of compost in the garden, involves your glutes, hamstrings, and back. Deadlifts strengthen all these muscles, explains Carr.

“They're a great way to build strength for everyday lifting, so those jobs feel easier and you're more confident handling heavier objects.”.

Rows are ideal for strengthening your upper back and arms, which we use for pulling movements throughout the day, from opening heavy doors to pulling a garden hose across the lawn.

Sources indicate that “They also help support good posture, particularly if you spend a lot of time sitting at a desk,” states Carr. “Using a resistance band makes it easy to adjust the difficulty as you get stronger.”.

Incline push-ups are a great way to build upper-body strength, working your chest, shoulders, arms, and core.

“These muscles help with everyday pushing movements, whether that's moving a shopping cart, pushing open a heavy door, or getting yourself up from the floor,” claims Carr.

They're also easy to adapt to your fitness level, so you can gradually increase the challenge as your strength improves.

We use rotational movements more than we probably realize, whether that's turning to put something in the back of the car, reaching across to pick something up or digging in the garden.

Woodchops are great for strengthening your core and improving your ability to twist and turn with control, Carr explains.

“That becomes particularly useful as we get older, helping us stay mobile and making everyday movements feel easier.”.

Industry observers note that kate puts together fitness content that covers functional and strength training, cardio, workout challenges, interviews and news. She's often doing gym laundry or listening to music.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • Industry observers note that TESTOSTERONE GOES BEYOND building muscle.
  • Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) can help raise T levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that TESTOSTERONE GOES BEYOND building muscle. T helps you maintain muscle mass, facial and body hair, sex drive, and red blood cell production. So when your T levels start to decline—which happens naturally in your thirties—there’s a whole range of symptoms like low libido or just feeling blue.

Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) can help raise T levels. After a couple of weeks to a month, you’ll start to see some changes, some substantial and small. Some pleasant and not so pleasant. Below, urologists explain what happens to your body a month after taking testosterone.

According to recent reports, IF YOU HAVE low T, your doctor will conduct some tests to see if you’re a good candidate for the therapy. Ryan Smith, MD, urologist specializing in men’s health at the University of Virginia Health, says a doctor will perform two blood tests in the morning (on different days) when testosterone is at its highest.

Low is considered under 300 nanograms per deciliter (ng/dL) by some accounts and under 264 ng/dL by others. Doctors also factor in any symptoms you’re having, like trouble getting erections or orgasms, fatigue, or just feeling blah.

Nowadays, testosterone is more accessible without a prescription, with many people only having to complete an online assessment. Leaving out a doctor’s approval and supervision, however, can be harmful, indicates Justin Dubin, MD, urologist at Baptist Health.

In a 2022 study that Dr. Dubin co-authored, researchers found that many online platforms are not providing testosterone therapy in accordance with the American Urological Association and the Endocrine Society guidelines. Using a secret shopper, the researchers found that the platforms offered therapy to men who didn’t meet the guidelines and didn’t mention the risks or benefits of testosterone therapy.

Industry observers note that working with a doctor ensures that you’re prescribed testosterone only when you need it and that you’re taking the right dose. Then, they can work with you to make sure your testosterone levels respond appropriately. Doctors like to recheck everything every six months to make sure you’re not having any negative side effects.

Recent findings suggest that A number of testosterone options are available. You can choose between injectables, topical gels, creams, under-the-skin pellet therapy, pills, and nasal sprays. You can learn more about them here.

In a recent development, each comes with its own set of side effects, so it all comes down to your personal preference, health situation, and what your insurance covers. You can read about the real-life experiences of guys of different ages and body types and their experiences with taking testosterone.

IT CAN TAKE a few weeks to a month or two to see your symptoms improve after starting testosterone replacement therapy, notes Dr. Smith. Here are some of the side effects—some obvious and some not—that come with testosterone therapy.

When you’re low on testosterone, you might notice your sex drive dip. But when you take TRT, the treatment reactivates the androgen receptors in the part of your brain that controls desire, states Abraham Morgentaler, MD, associate clinical professor of urology at Harvard Medical School and author of Testosterone for Life. Regaining a healthy sex drive is one of the biggest benefits of testosterone replacement therapy, he says.

TRT may also make your erections more satisfying, though this isn’t the only piece of the puzzle. Erections also rely on healthy nerves and blood flow. That means that testosterone therapy by itself won't always help erectile dysfunction.

It has been revealed that muscles respond to testosterone and starting TRT can increase muscle mass, says Dr. Morgentaler. That’s because testosterone activates the androgen receptors in muscle tissue to stimulate growth.

The effect of a testosterone replacement dose on your muscles, however, is fairly minimal. To make the most of this muscle-building benefit, you’ll need to be doing your part through strength training and possibly raising the amount of protein you consume (depending on your current intake). Don’t know where to start? Check out MH’s four-week muscle building guide.

Some men also report fat loss. While testosterone doesn’t directly incite fat loss itself, part of it may be thanks to the uptick in muscle mass. The more muscle you have, the higher your basal metabolic rate (BMR). That means your body will burn more calories at rest.

Sources indicate that another indirect way testosterone can help with fat loss is motivation to keep pushing once you see results. Jed Kaminetsky, MD, urologist at NYU Langone Medical Center, testosterone can increase your energy levels, making it easier to get up and sweat it out.

Sources indicate that fatigue is a common symptom of low T. “When we treat them, a lot of men will say that their energy has improved,” says Dr. Morgentaler.

Sources indicate that scientists studying testosterone aren't sure exactly how the hormone plays a role in energy—just that it does. One of the prevailing hypotheses Dr. Morgentaler can get behind is that testosterone somehow affects your mitochondria (that organelle you learned in high school is the powerhouse of your cells). The theory is that “testosterone turns them on, so they're more productive in terms of creating the energy that the cells need.”.

Ronald Tamler, MD, PhD, associate professor of medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, notes changes in energy may also be tied back to androgen receptors. “If they don't get sufficient input, that can cause fatigue,” he says. Bringing testosterone levels back up can help reverse this.

It has been revealed that experts don't have a definitive answer to why testosterone impacts mood so deeply—after all, “the brain is a complicated thing,” notes Dr. Tamler. But the positive effect of TRT on mood is a potential life-changing benefit.

An old but highly referenced clinical trial in 2003 looked at how testosterone gels affected middle-aged men with treatment-resistant depression and low T. After 8 weeks, the men showed greater improvements in the psychological aspects of depression (sadness, guilt, and anxiety) than those given a placebo. The men taking testosterone gels also showed nearly the same rate of improvement in somatic aspects of depression (improvements in sleep, appetite, and libido). A more recent review of 27 clinical trials involving 1,890 men with low T found that TRT provided a significant reduction in depressive symptoms, especially at higher doses.

One of the most vital things to know before starting TRT is that the treatment decreases sperm production and may cause infertility.

Testosterone might affect the size of your testicles, too. "Most of the size of the testicle is dedicated to making sperm, so when you're making less sperm, the testicles get smaller," says Dr. Morgentaler.

In a recent development, sperm production may or may not go back to normal even after stopping treatment, claims Dr. Kaminetsky. One study found increasing age and longer TRT linked to lower chances of normal sperm recovery.

In a recent development, some people notice a little swelling in their feet and ankles because testosterone can encourage your body to hold onto excess fluid, claims Dr. Morgentaler.

This isn't a big deal for most people, he claims, and swelling is more common if you're taking a non-daily treatment like an injection, when you're getting a higher dose of T in one sitting.

Testosterone replacement therapy may change your skin type—for better or for worse, claims Dr. Morgentaler.

It has been revealed that testosterone can increase oil production, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. Oil production is vital for healthy skin, so you may actually end up with a better complexion. However, too much oily buildup can lead to breakouts.

While Dr. Morgentaler notes testosterone-induced breakouts aren’t common, they are more likely to occur in men with a history of acne. Skin changes may also be more common if you’re taking testosterone injections versus other modes of administration since you're getting a higher dose all at once.

Industry observers note that in all men—whether you’re taking T or not—some testosterone is converted into the hormone estradiol, a form of estrogen. In men who naturally have more breast tissue, testosterone can be converted into estradiol, which may stimulate breast tissue to grow.

In a recent development, this is called gynecomastia, says Dr. Morgentaler, and it's not as common as other side effects. If gynecomastia does happen, your doctor will likely stop treatment for a month or two to allow your breast tissue to go back to normal. Then, you’ll resume T along with a drug that blocks the conversion of testosterone to estradiol.

If you’re going the topical testosterone therapy route, one issue to watch out for is transference with women and children.

Darshan Patel, MD, assistant professor of urology at the University of California San Diego’s Men’s Health Center, states testosterone from gels or creams can be transferred through skin-to-skin contact or from clothing and absorbed by someone else.

“You really have to be careful to wash your hands well and not expose others,” adds Dr. Smith. Contact with excess testosterone can affect children’s genitalia and cause premature pubic hair development and aggressive behavior.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Around the world, the number of uncontacted Indigenous tribes continues to dwindle.
  • On November 17, the nonprofit advocacy group Survival International reported a recent incident in which 20 members of the Awá people intentionally contacted local government officials in the Brazilian Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around the world, the number of uncontacted Indigenous tribes continues to dwindle. Indigenous rights advocates estimate that half of the nearly 200 communities still existing in comparative isolation could disappear within a decade, without proper safeguards against climate change, land loss, fame-seeking opportunists, and illegal industrial encroachments. Unfortunately, the situation has apparently grown so dire that some Indigenous groups are reaching out for help—and exposing themselves to potentially deadly foreign diseases in the process.

On November 17, the nonprofit advocacy group Survival International reported a recent incident in which 20 members of the Awá people intentionally contacted local government officials in the Brazilian Amazon. Although proficient hunter-gatherers, the group requested yams before taking them back into the rainforest.

“This is a troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger,” Survival International director Caroline Pearce noted in a statement.

Sources indicate that the Awá are one of the world’s last uncontacted Indigenous tribes, whose ties to the Brazilian rainforest stretch back centuries. They faced their first attacks from European settlers during the 1800s, which eventually forced them to adopt a nomadic lifestyle to avoid future encounters. Brazil finally supplied the Awá with settlement areas during the mid-1980s, but it still took years before the government properly invested in demarcated land. In the meantime, numerous deadly interactions with loggers, farmers, and other illegal intruders had reduced the Awá community to barely 300 people. Of those, advocates estimate only about one-third of the hunter-gatherers remain completely isolated from the outside world.

“The Brazilian government must commit the resources necessary to protect [the region of] Arariboia from the loggers and ranchers who are razing it, in flagrant defiance of the law,” Pearce added.

Sources indicate that in addition to the advocacy work by Survival International, the Awá are supported by a team of Indigenous members of the Guajajara community known as the Forest Guardians. These volunteers have spent years pushing back against illegal cattle ranchers and loggers attempting to claim land in Arariboia, often dying as a result of their efforts.

“The Forest Guardians have always worked to protect the Awá against encroachment, even at the cost of losing warriors in battle,” the organization remarked. “We demand immediate action from the relevant authorities…to ensure what the Awá believe is best for them, safeguarding their lives, health, safety and dignity. FOR THE AWÁ, FOR THE TENETEHAR [language], AND FOR THE FOREST!”.

Energy Drinks, Stimulant Supplements Linked to Higher Heart Risks in Young Adults
